3	## Paper 2 Instructions

16	1,400 - 1,800 words
17	
18	For this assignment, find and close read two texts that (1) have a substantial relationship between them and (2) are related to the topical interest of this module. Write an essay in which you establish a clear and interesting connection between the two and provide an argument that rationalizes this relationship.
19	
20	In paper 1, you were asked to write a close reading essay that attempted to find, within a given text, an issue or problem that might be of interest to your reader. You were also asked to locate the evidence of this problem from within the text and to show how the evidence could present a resolution to the problem. While this essay aimed at getting you to practise some basic rhetorical skills of writing as well as critical reading and thinking skills, it was admittedly a difficult assignment. This is especially so since the nature of academic writing is seldom so involuted: most academic writing expect your evidence to come from a wide range of sources.
21	
22	For paper 2, we will now begin to look for evidence elsewhere and to practise incorporating this evidence into an argument needed to support the thesis of a close reading essay. So to a large extent, this assignment should be seen as an extension of paper 1. In most respects you will, as in paper one, need to find an interesting problem or puzzle (motive) and to propose to your readers what is significant about this or how it might be resolved (thesis). However, unlike the first paper, what you will be doing here is to develop your motive and thesis based on two texts. There are two different ways of doing so, and they are explained below.
23	
24	Lens Analysis vs Comparative Analysis
25	In a lens analysis, the problem or puzzle comes from the first (which we can call the primary) text. Oftentimes, the resolution or explanation of this problem may not exist within the primary text itself. So you will have to find this by looking at another text (the secondary text). This secondary text may already have explicit arguments made regarding your primary text or may provide more implicit theory that will help you make sense of the first. Hence, in a lens analysis, the secondary text acts as a ?lens? that helps you clarify or formulate thoughts about the primary text.
26	
27	In a comparative analysis, you will also be working with two primary sources and using both to help you come up with a motive. In order to do this, you compare and contrast the texts with each other, so much so that it is only after close reading the texts that you can then identify the interest, puzzle, or problem. Since you aren't using a third (or more) source at this point, the thesis will also be derived from your observations of these two sources.
28

Comments for week 7 presentations

Group 1: Rahul, Manae, Emma, Ziheng ("Stop Vaping")
This is an excellent choice in texts for a comparative analysis. The grounds for comparison (GFC) are stable and justified, so it is the national background that serves as why the texts are significant. From a content perspective, there are many similarities between them, but yet as you point out, there are important differences as well, which you note in the two sub-arguments your group suggested. 
There are still quite a few things that I should point out, some of which might have already been mentioned in class:
Further considering the GFC: I mentioned that comparing the two text has significance because it tells us something about the underlying cultures. Broadly, how a Western liberal society and a "conservative Asian" (for want of a better word) society handles anti-vaping campaigns. The reason why this is interesting is because liberal societies believe that the individual has rights and the government has no business taking away those rights, unless it impacts on other people. This is why these societies can be more restrictive when it comes to smoking. One's right to smoke cannot come at the expense of other people who don't want to be exposed to side-stream smoke. This leads to a greater international consensus on banning smoking from many public spaces. But since vaping has none or less of this kind of impact, the liberal mindset is that individuals will need to self-regulate (much like other kinds of addiction like drinking and gambling). Then, this leads us to ask, why then are places like Singapore so much more restrictive. Of course, all this doesn't need to go into your "essay", but it's essential to be aware of this because this can then shape your comparative analysis (some of this might be relevant to your essay context -- see below).
Frame of reference: This wasn't mentioned specifically in the slides (and presentation?), but it will be good to identify this. Is it going to be about youth culture (since this is the common target audience)? Mode of persuasion? Or liberalism vs conservatism (you can imagine the title of the essay: "Liberalism and conservatism in recent anti-vaping campaign ads").
Context and Motive: You also didn't specify this, and it would be good. It would be good to know what the M is, given a T that still feels quite general now. The C might be something like this: "Unlike smoking, where there is greater international consensus about its regulation and exclusion from public spaces, vaping is subjected to substantially different treatments in places like Australia and Singapore..." This then allows you to raise nationally-based questions that go on to justify why these texts (for e.g. in Australia, vaping is treated like other permitted vices like drinking and gambling where state and civil society step in to discourage such practices, as compared with outright outlawing in Sg). I hope you see where this is headed. Then, for the M, you should see if there is any observation you can make that allows you to raise the question.
Sub-arguments and further closer reading: This is the nicest thing about your presentation. You've got two very workable sub-arguments that show good close reading. I get what you mean by "aggressive" vs "gradual" but I'm not sure if these are the best choice of words. There's still more close reading you can do. What's interesting about the SG one is that it is presented like a movie trailer, complete with the familiar rating card at the beginning (you mentioned this), and the same cinematic effects we find in the trailer for a horror film. What's interesting is how the trailer is subverted in the end -- the narrator tells us that everything in the trailer isn't a movie but is real. What can we do with this observation? Then, there is the social aspect of the Australian one (you pointed this out, so excellent), but what about the end frame. In fact, do think about the end frames -- they play a crucial role in campaign ads because this is where the final message (warning, instruction) is presented. In the Australian one, it says "Let's join the thousands quitting vapes." It's hopeful but re-socializes. If the ad shows the increasing ostracization of youth vapers because of their habits, the last frame implies finding a new community (of vape quitters). For the SG: it's "The horrors of vaping are real. Stop vape. Don't wait." For a communitarian society, it's interesting that it individualizes the action (do it for yourself) -- the Australian one seems more communitarian. These are just some examples, so with more time you can develop more detailed aspects of the close reading.

Group 2 (Alex, Joshua, Samuel, Rei)"Exploring Depictions of Yellow Peril in 19th Century Australia and United States"
This is the first set of slides that I am responding too, so the things I say initially will have broader relevance to all groups particularly surrounding the texts that you select for comparative analysis and the approach you might take. The initial concerns will normally be grounds for comparison (GFC) and frame of reference (FOR). In the GFC you'll need to make sure that the reason why you've chosen the texts is justifiable and stable. There is always a deeper implication for the selection -- looking at the texts tells us something interesting in comparing the contexts. Perhaps, the texts tell us differences or surprising similarities in the historical, cultural, or national contexts. You'll need to also make sure there aren't too many variables otherwise the comparison becomes untenable. For example, try to avoid texts that are both different historically and culturall, otherwise you can't fully justify why you are comparing those texts. 
As for the FOR, you'll need to be focused. See if you can find a concept or a useful key term to establish the angle you can use to frame your view of the texts. This particularly vital if the scope of your texts is big (especially if your are working with books, films, or even entire TV series). As long as you have a well-defined and justified FOR, readers won't need you to tell them every detail of the texts. Of course, if you can bring in lens texts, you'll have a solid basis for introducing this concept. This is something you can aim to do as you move into paper 3, but in paper 2 (since you'll mainly be looking at two primary texts) you'll need to rely more on an intuited concept. This is why more generalized FORs like power, patriarchy, capitalism, racism, sexism can be useful. If you deploy them intuitively and especially in a well-considered way, the FOR will work.
Back to this group specifically, the GFC is mostly stable,  with the main implication of the comparison being national (how might Australia's be different from America's). There could potentially be a complication, which is the nature of the texts. One of them is an editorial cartoon, while the other is an advertisement for a commercial product. This isn't too much of problem (and I think your group might have acknowledged that), but this is where you'll have an opportunity for an acknowledgement/response in your argumentation -- regardless of mode, they still are based on the same underlying racial tension in similar white settler societies. As for the FOR, this can still be further considered. Right now, you've got power dynamics. This makes sense. Essentially, both texts exhibit issues surrounding this because they represent power-related tensions exhibited within the content and on the wider contextual level. Within the content, we can see how they are different (powerful Asians in the cartoon, weak Asians in the ad); but on the contextual level they presume similar white authorship and readership, and so the Chinese are still in the same pejorative way regardless on how they are framed specifically in the content). While this works, there can still be other possibilities, apart from power, such as race/racism, white superiority. Since your title already brings in the issue of Yellow Peril, then it makes sense that race should be brought in as the FOR.
I should also make a comment about the "prospective paper". I didn't mention the requirement of the CMT and the paper's argumentation in my instructions for the presentation prep. That's because I was hoping that it would potentially be the class effort to help identify these after the presentation. But then before the presentation I sent an email to say that it might be good if the groups could start thinking about these as well. So, I'm glad that your group considered these. The M makes perfect sense: this is something noticeable -- why does one portray the Chinese and powerful, dangerous, while the other as weak. Yet at the same time, there is something that fundamentally normalizes things -- the Chinese as the Other. So ultimately, the Australian text calls for action, while the American one shows the consequences of action (successful eviction of the Chinese through the application of technology). Consequently, this then leads to the thesis about the "paradoxical other". In racial politics, representing the racial other as both powerful and weak are interestingly not a contradiction in terms but co-facilitative aspects in the representation of the other. If your paper were to be further developed as paper 3, then you might want to bring in lens texts like Abdul JanMohamed and his concept of the Manichean allegory, or Edward Said's concept of manifest vs latent Orientalism. My own concept of "disjuncture" tries to unify these concepts, and you can find this in my earliest book The Disjunctive Empire of International Relations (chapter 2).
Now, I don't think your group specifically explained how the argumentation will look like; in other words how you might make use of the sub-arguments to support the thesis. The discussion of the FOR does give us a hint, though. It looks like you will first explore the differences between the text, but then go on to find similarities. The similarities will then be tied to broader intuitive understandings of racial politics in both societies and thus used as the unifying element (the material that helps to resolve the paradox/contradiction).
Anyway, an excellent job here. This looks promising if it were to be turned into a real paper 2.

Group 3: Hongrui, Kai Li, Yixiang, Zi Yue ("WW2 'Home Front' Propaganda")
The point of the presentation was to get us thinking about how we might do a comparative analysis that would lead nicely to the requirements of paper 2. So as I explained in some of the comments I left for the other groups, the main expectations were for the presentation to show what your starting processes would have been like in doing a comparative analysis between two selected texts. Of course, if you were able to also start thinking about the possible CMT and the sub-arguments, that would also be wonderful. Even if you didn't do this, the goal would be for the rest of the class to see if they could help come up with these. Thus, your presentation mainly showed the starting processes and less of the possibilities of the resulting paper.
As I mentioned in class, there are the two elements crucial to the starting process -- identifying your grounds for comparison (GFC) and frame of reference (FOR). Both of these will give you some discipline on how to focus on the text and not end up with a series of banal comparisons. There are strong possibilities for these. The GFC is clear: both of these are "food security" texts employed during the similar time frame in the second world war. And there are a lot of similarities as your group pointing out, especially with the promise of bountiful food and the role of women. Sometimes it's also good to have differences, because these can be instructive and they offer you the significance. For example if they are set in different eras but in the same place and subject matter, they offer us a chance to talk about what has changed historically. In this case, the contextual difference is slight, and this is the campaigns to promote victory gardens and food preservation. The FOR, however, is much more clearly stated. So we have mention of the two campaigns, the role of civilians, and more significantly women's role. What I found surprising was the omission of what your title suggested. In this sense, the place of "home front" is another FOR. Remember, we spoke about this in class since the outbreak of the War redrew the boundaries between private and public, and between "home" and outside spaces. Awareness of this and the new roles women were expected to play in the new home front could be the immediate contextualization you establish in your essay.
As for the close reading, your group has made some workable and important observations, such as the texts' refusal to engage with the issue of wartime scarcity/austerity, how domestic activities are reframed as patriotic efforts. So the points you made about similarities and differences are good. But, all these are just the starting point for what could be a paper. How then will you make use of these similarities and differences? Are there other details that your close reading may not have considered? For example, in the war gardens poster, the woman wears a military cap -- can this be used in anyway? She's also standing in a soldierly position, and the hoe almost resembles a rifle that soldiers are normally photographed with. What about the bright sunshine, the light blue background, and the red, white and blue palette? Then, for the other text, there is the same background colour, but the woman's demeanour is different. In fact it is something that is more remarkable than the other -- how do we interpret her posture and interaction with the audience (she is addressing viewers directly)?
Finally, there are still the CMT and sub-arguments to develop. In class, we thought of some possibilities including contradictions in objectives. For instance, why are these texts promoting consumption when it is normally more about austerity and discipline? Perhaps the M can be something to do with women's roles? Or about contradictions in what the texts' objectives might otherwise be?
PM 
Group 1: Athyna, Bethany, Fang Hong, Mona (Anti-drugs campaign texts)
Many thanks for preparing the very detailed class handout. It was very useful as it complemented what you presented on the slides and it offered much more insight into your close reading of the two texts. 
As you know, I raised some initial issues about the grounds for comparison (GFC) not being stable, plus a few other things, but let me leave that aside for now and just go with what you got. From this perspective, it would be a very interesting selection because they represent two different approaches to the anti-drug message. When you select the texts from two places (SG and HK), the implication is that you want to direct readers' attention to possibly national differences. This is further brought up in your T (the notion of different "imagined citizens"). So bringing up HK's approach is fascinating. In fact, when I saw it, my first impression was: is this for real? Are they trivializing things since drug consumption has consequences far worse than one's beauty. But then as I thought about it, I began to see the genius and the ability to understand youth psychology. For young people, death is too unreal a threat to dangle, something like tarnished looks is a more tangible and immediate thing to worry about. This then makes it worthwhile situating it against the more traditional one we find in the SG text.
Now, while I do like the observations you made in your close reading (especially what you have in your handout), there are some fundamental issues to think about:

GFC: There are some instabilities with too many variables. You should try to cut it back to one (either the national difference in the same era or historical differences in the same place). There are other variables. For example, audience. The HK text addresses drug takers. But the SG text, as you mentioned, is directed at people who might potentially attend the workshop, these aren't drug takers but members of the public who want to be more informed (family members, support people?). Another variable is the objective of the message. The direct intention of the HK text is to discourage drug consumption. For the SG text, it's to encourage viewers to attend the workshop. But given these variables it might still be possible to stabilize things. This means -- you'll need a darn good acknowledgement/reasoning set. Another possibility is to shift the weighting of the texts. You can make HK text the main text of the paper, and the motive comes mainly from this text (doesn't this text trivialize the dangers of drug consumption?), and the SG text can be weighted less and used as an example of the traditional messaging found in most anti-drug campaigns.
FOR: It would be good to find a more conceptually-driven FOR. The ones you pointed out on the slide seem to be more related to your GFC. So something more appropriate might be "ugliness as deterrence". Or focus on "waste": the waste of a life vs the waste of good looks. Or you can bring in "fear" as another possibility.
Thesis: Be careful with the first part to your thesis, which abstracts away from the text and focuses on national differences. When you say "the difference in fear mechanism employed is indicative of the state having a specific imagined citizens", my first reaction is: can you argue this just by looking at the texts? We cannot conclusively say so just from textual evidence. So you can make this more about what the texts are doing. Thus, rewriting the T in your handout, we have "I argue that the difference in fear mechanism employed implies that each texts has a different view of the imagined citizen". The difference here is that we are saying that it implies that the text is doing this rather than the state is.

You might also want to check out the presentation by group 1 from the morning class and the comments I left for them. They also did something similar with anti-vaping campaigns.

Group 2: An, Isaac, Si Xuan, Wayne (AIDS campaign texts)
Thanks for the presentation. Your group was mindful to present a bit of everything, including the decisions you made surrounding the starting processes (frame of reference, reasons for selecting the texts, preliminary observations), as well as the more prospective processes of writing what might end up being a paper. In this case, the motive, thesis, and sub-arguments. There was one additional element, which was the grounds for comparison (GFC). While you didn't point them out specifically, they were implied in many places, such as in the FOR section. But, in any event, the GFC is clear especially in the slides on the major differences (ironically some of these differences were similarities too). Too any viewer, there are obvious connections, and this is why a comparative analysis is possible and justified.
There were also some interesting observations in your close reading. I particularly like the sensitivity you showed with the obvious association of AIDS with death. But how this association is made is different. One is ignorance, while the other is silence. And this then connects individual responsibility with social responsibility.  What's interesting especially with the US text is its greater obtrusiveness. While the UK text's message is immediately clear, especially for us viewing the text now, the US text is mysterious. Why is "silence = death"? For those who are not familiar with ACT UP or their campaign, the answer isn't provided easily. The only thing they have to go with is the body copy in very small font. In fact, you don't get an answer. Readers are greeted by even more questions, and then a call to action. So silence here does not literally mean being quiet but not acting, and the call to action indirectly suggests that government action is causing death. Again, recalling the messaging of danger in disease texts, what's deadly isn't the disease itself but the government and other institutions. So I'm digressing a bit, but clearly the second text is much more interesting. Perhaps, one possibility is to "weight" (I'm using this as a verb) the US text more. It's even possible to develop the motive solely out of this text alone, and then bring in the second text as the contextual background (why if the AIDS campaigns often focus on the relationship between patients and disease, do we get a text that re-establishes a different relationship?). Any way, the point I'm making is that there are good close reading observations, such as in the differences table and the sub-arguments you make.
What's more important is to point out some issues with your close reading, comparative analysis, and prospects for the essay:

FOR: You might have confused this with your GFC. As mentioned, the FOR should be more conceptually driven, and this will give you focus and an angle. Perhaps, it can be the tensions between individualism (UK) and social/political responsibility (US). Or the politicization of the discourse on AIDS, as opposed to the traditional medicalization.
Thesis: What you've got now is captured in one of the FORs mentioned above. But you'll need to review some of the things you mentioned. I read the first sentence a few times and something sounds off. The second phrase "their different intended audiences produced different...". It sounds as if the essay will focus on the audience. But you don't have any material on the audience. The thesis should come back to what the texts are doing and not what its audience is doing. 

That's all I have for now. One quick final point -- good job with explaining the pink triangle, it raises an interesting point about how the movement is indirectly associating things with genocide by drawing references to the holocaust. This is obviously a text that doesn't explain itself but perhaps encourages curious individuals to go find out more.

Group 3: Ian, Ashley, Aidan ("Anti-VD")
Thanks for going beyond the initial instructions by spending more time to develop what could potentially be the motive, thesis, and the corresponding sub-arguments for a paper that could emerge from this comparative analysis. Interestingly, what really caught my attention was the process-oriented nature of the argumentation, rather than an argumentation that is simply list oriented. By process-oriented I'm referring to an argument that builds on the previous, so in this case you go from how the texts lull male viewers into a sense of security, how they then subvert that, and then lead to the invoking of fear and paranoia of women. Working backwards, I can see how this might address your thesis on how the texts might be effective in meeting their objectives, and how the thesis responds to the question about why are the texts presented in their corresponding ways instead of the expected provision of medical information.
Now, I feel less concerned about the sub-arguments as I am with the M and T. I think a stronger case can be made for the M, because I don't feel the assumption that the texts should communicate medical information is sufficiently justified. Yes, we know that oftentimes public health campaigns provide medical information, but that's not always the case. Public health campaigns often adopt a wide variety of approaches and employing tactics other than medicalization is not uncommon. We need more justification here. Why not find a problem that is much more within the texts themselves, rather than connecting them to contextual assumptions? Then, I'm also worried about the T especially when the "effectiveness" argument is made. If you want to do this you'll need to spend some time to explain what constitutes effectiveness in this case and what standards you apply to measure it. This cannot be assumed intuitively. Alternatively, why not identify a more precise T that deals with something generally observed. For example, "I argue that it simultaneously empowers and disempowers women through a three-step process..." This way you sidestep the problem of explaining why the texts could be "effective". Although you'll now need to see if the sub-arguments still work.
Now some additional points. Coming back to GFC -- that seems stable, so no issues there. The FOR feels more generic now, so there could be something more specific, perhaps along the lines of the villainization of women or patriarchy? Finally, just a quibble over the interpretation of the first "Loaded?" and the gun in the second text. I've been wondering about this for a long time, but my sense is that the gun isn't meant to be threatening but as a visual metaphor for male sexual power. That explains why the first "Loaded" is actually directed at the male viewer (it actually means "Are you loaded?"), and this explains why then it says that women are "also loaded". The key word here is "also", thus interestingly it coevals male power with female power. Perhaps this can be a way to establish the motive?

Comments for week 7 presentations
AM section
Group 1: Rahul, Manae, Emma, Ziheng ("Stop Vaping")
This is an excellent choice in texts for a comparative analysis. The grounds for comparison (GFC) are stable and justified, so it is the national background that serves as why the texts are significant. From a content perspective, there are many similarities between them, but yet as you point out, there are important differences as well, which you note in the two sub-arguments your group suggested. 
There are still quite a few things that I should point out, some of which might have already been mentioned in class:
Further considering the GFC: I mentioned that comparing the two text has significance because it tells us something about the underlying cultures. Broadly, how a Western liberal society and a "conservative Asian" (for want of a better word) society handles anti-vaping campaigns. The reason why this is interesting is because liberal societies believe that the individual has rights and the government has no business taking away those rights, unless it impacts on other people. This is why these societies can be more restrictive when it comes to smoking. One's right to smoke cannot come at the expense of other people who don't want to be exposed to side-stream smoke. This leads to a greater international consensus on banning smoking from many public spaces. But since vaping has none or less of this kind of impact, the liberal mindset is that individuals will need to self-regulate (much like other kinds of addiction like drinking and gambling). Then, this leads us to ask, why then are places like Singapore so much more restrictive. Of course, all this doesn't need to go into your "essay", but it's essential to be aware of this because this can then shape your comparative analysis (some of this might be relevant to your essay context -- see below).
Frame of reference: This wasn't mentioned specifically in the slides (and presentation?), but it will be good to identify this. Is it going to be about youth culture (since this is the common target audience)? Mode of persuasion? Or liberalism vs conservatism (you can imagine the title of the essay: "Liberalism and conservatism in recent anti-vaping campaign ads").
Context and Motive: You also didn't specify this, and it would be good. It would be good to know what the M is, given a T that still feels quite general now. The C might be something like this: "Unlike smoking, where there is greater international consensus about its regulation and exclusion from public spaces, vaping is subjected to substantially different treatments in places like Australia and Singapore..." This then allows you to raise nationally-based questions that go on to justify why these texts (for e.g. in Australia, vaping is treated like other permitted vices like drinking and gambling where state and civil society step in to discourage such practices, as compared with outright outlawing in Sg). I hope you see where this is headed. Then, for the M, you should see if there is any observation you can make that allows you to raise the question.
Sub-arguments and further closer reading: This is the nicest thing about your presentation. You've got two very workable sub-arguments that show good close reading. I get what you mean by "aggressive" vs "gradual" but I'm not sure if these are the best choice of words. There's still more close reading you can do. What's interesting about the SG one is that it is presented like a movie trailer, complete with the familiar rating card at the beginning (you mentioned this), and the same cinematic effects we find in the trailer for a horror film. What's interesting is how the trailer is subverted in the end -- the narrator tells us that everything in the trailer isn't a movie but is real. What can we do with this observation? Then, there is the social aspect of the Australian one (you pointed this out, so excellent), but what about the end frame. In fact, do think about the end frames -- they play a crucial role in campaign ads because this is where the final message (warning, instruction) is presented. In the Australian one, it says "Let's join the thousands quitting vapes." It's hopeful but re-socializes. If the ad shows the increasing ostracization of youth vapers because of their habits, the last frame implies finding a new community (of vape quitters). For the SG: it's "The horrors of vaping are real. Stop vape. Don't wait." For a communitarian society, it's interesting that it individualizes the action (do it for yourself) -- the Australian one seems more communitarian. These are just some examples, so with more time you can develop more detailed aspects of the close reading.

Group 2 (Alex, Joshua, Samuel, Rei)"Exploring Depictions of Yellow Peril in 19th Century Australia and United States"
This is the first set of slides that I am responding too, so the things I say initially will have broader relevance to all groups particularly surrounding the texts that you select for comparative analysis and the approach you might take. The initial concerns will normally be grounds for comparison (GFC) and frame of reference (FOR). In the GFC you'll need to make sure that the reason why you've chosen the texts is justifiable and stable. There is always a deeper implication for the selection -- looking at the texts tells us something interesting in comparing the contexts. Perhaps, the texts tell us differences or surprising similarities in the historical, cultural, or national contexts. You'll need to also make sure there aren't too many variables otherwise the comparison becomes untenable. For example, try to avoid texts that are both different historically and culturall, otherwise you can't fully justify why you are comparing those texts. 
As for the FOR, you'll need to be focused. See if you can find a concept or a useful key term to establish the angle you can use to frame your view of the texts. This particularly vital if the scope of your texts is big (especially if your are working with books, films, or even entire TV series). As long as you have a well-defined and justified FOR, readers won't need you to tell them every detail of the texts. Of course, if you can bring in lens texts, you'll have a solid basis for introducing this concept. This is something you can aim to do as you move into paper 3, but in paper 2 (since you'll mainly be looking at two primary texts) you'll need to rely more on an intuited concept. This is why more generalized FORs like power, patriarchy, capitalism, racism, sexism can be useful. If you deploy them intuitively and especially in a well-considered way, the FOR will work.
Back to this group specifically, the GFC is mostly stable,  with the main implication of the comparison being national (how might Australia's be different from America's). There could potentially be a complication, which is the nature of the texts. One of them is an editorial cartoon, while the other is an advertisement for a commercial product. This isn't too much of problem (and I think your group might have acknowledged that), but this is where you'll have an opportunity for an acknowledgement/response in your argumentation -- regardless of mode, they still are based on the same underlying racial tension in similar white settler societies. As for the FOR, this can still be further considered. Right now, you've got power dynamics. This makes sense. Essentially, both texts exhibit issues surrounding this because they represent power-related tensions exhibited within the content and on the wider contextual level. Within the content, we can see how they are different (powerful Asians in the cartoon, weak Asians in the ad); but on the contextual level they presume similar white authorship and readership, and so the Chinese are still in the same pejorative way regardless on how they are framed specifically in the content). While this works, there can still be other possibilities, apart from power, such as race/racism, white superiority. Since your title already brings in the issue of Yellow Peril, then it makes sense that race should be brought in as the FOR.
I should also make a comment about the "prospective paper". I didn't mention the requirement of the CMT and the paper's argumentation in my instructions for the presentation prep. That's because I was hoping that it would potentially be the class effort to help identify these after the presentation. But then before the presentation I sent an email to say that it might be good if the groups could start thinking about these as well. So, I'm glad that your group considered these. The M makes perfect sense: this is something noticeable -- why does one portray the Chinese and powerful, dangerous, while the other as weak. Yet at the same time, there is something that fundamentally normalizes things -- the Chinese as the Other. So ultimately, the Australian text calls for action, while the American one shows the consequences of action (successful eviction of the Chinese through the application of technology). Consequently, this then leads to the thesis about the "paradoxical other". In racial politics, representing the racial other as both powerful and weak are interestingly not a contradiction in terms but co-facilitative aspects in the representation of the other. If your paper were to be further developed as paper 3, then you might want to bring in lens texts like Abdul JanMohamed and his concept of the Manichean allegory, or Edward Said's concept of manifest vs latent Orientalism. My own concept of "disjuncture" tries to unify these concepts, and you can find this in my earliest book The Disjunctive Empire of International Relations (chapter 2).
Now, I don't think your group specifically explained how the argumentation will look like; in other words how you might make use of the sub-arguments to support the thesis. The discussion of the FOR does give us a hint, though. It looks like you will first explore the differences between the text, but then go on to find similarities. The similarities will then be tied to broader intuitive understandings of racial politics in both societies and thus used as the unifying element (the material that helps to resolve the paradox/contradiction).
Anyway, an excellent job here. This looks promising if it were to be turned into a real paper 2.

Group 3: Hongrui, Kai Li, Yixiang, Zi Yue ("WW2 'Home Front' Propaganda")
The point of the presentation was to get us thinking about how we might do a comparative analysis that would lead nicely to the requirements of paper 2. So as I explained in some of the comments I left for the other groups, the main expectations were for the presentation to show what your starting processes would have been like in doing a comparative analysis between two selected texts. Of course, if you were able to also start thinking about the possible CMT and the sub-arguments, that would also be wonderful. Even if you didn't do this, the goal would be for the rest of the class to see if they could help come up with these. Thus, your presentation mainly showed the starting processes and less of the possibilities of the resulting paper.
As I mentioned in class, there are the two elements crucial to the starting process -- identifying your grounds for comparison (GFC) and frame of reference (FOR). Both of these will give you some discipline on how to focus on the text and not end up with a series of banal comparisons. There are strong possibilities for these. The GFC is clear: both of these are "food security" texts employed during the similar time frame in the second world war. And there are a lot of similarities as your group pointing out, especially with the promise of bountiful food and the role of women. Sometimes it's also good to have differences, because these can be instructive and they offer you the significance. For example if they are set in different eras but in the same place and subject matter, they offer us a chance to talk about what has changed historically. In this case, the contextual difference is slight, and this is the campaigns to promote victory gardens and food preservation. The FOR, however, is much more clearly stated. So we have mention of the two campaigns, the role of civilians, and more significantly women's role. What I found surprising was the omission of what your title suggested. In this sense, the place of "home front" is another FOR. Remember, we spoke about this in class since the outbreak of the War redrew the boundaries between private and public, and between "home" and outside spaces. Awareness of this and the new roles women were expected to play in the new home front could be the immediate contextualization you establish in your essay.
As for the close reading, your group has made some workable and important observations, such as the texts' refusal to engage with the issue of wartime scarcity/austerity, how domestic activities are reframed as patriotic efforts. So the points you made about similarities and differences are good. But, all these are just the starting point for what could be a paper. How then will you make use of these similarities and differences? Are there other details that your close reading may not have considered? For example, in the war gardens poster, the woman wears a military cap -- can this be used in anyway? She's also standing in a soldierly position, and the hoe almost resembles a rifle that soldiers are normally photographed with. What about the bright sunshine, the light blue background, and the red, white and blue palette? Then, for the other text, there is the same background colour, but the woman's demeanour is different. In fact it is something that is more remarkable than the other -- how do we interpret her posture and interaction with the audience (she is addressing viewers directly)?
Finally, there are still the CMT and sub-arguments to develop. In class, we thought of some possibilities including contradictions in objectives. For instance, why are these texts promoting consumption when it is normally more about austerity and discipline? Perhaps the M can be something to do with women's roles? Or about contradictions in what the texts' objectives might otherwise be?
PM

# Meeting 5A (Thinking with Writing: Danger and Security)

Source: course site lesson page, saved 7 Oct 2026. Links are as published on the page.

### Week 5: Meeting 5A
**Unit 2 introduction/Comparative and lens analyses**  
Sep 8, 2026

## Class Activities

- Discuss what is in store for unit 2: rhetorical and topical issues
- Discuss readings assigned for this lesson (see below)

## Preparations
For this lesson, be sure to read the following (you can download them by clicking on the respective links):

- "Draped in the American Flag: Cold War Liberals and the Resistance to Theory" (pp. 19-26) [[download](https://dns.teachsystems.com/viewobj.cfm?id=55)
]

- "Reconstructing Homosexuality: Hitchcock and Homoerotics of Spectatorial Pleasure" (pp. 56-61) [[download](https://dns.teachsystems.com/viewobj.cfm?id=54)
].

Both items are chapters (or parts) of Robert J. Corber, In the Name of National Security: Hitchcock, Homophobia, and the Political Construction of Gender in Postwar America (Durham: Duke U. P., 1993). Now, when reading these items, please don't feel initimidated by the theoretical complexity (especially the psychoanalytic concepts in the second reading) presented. Essentially, we want to use these chapters as a way of approaching the issue of national security in an unconventional way. Oftentimes, homosexuality, the accompanying homophobia, and fiction (such as the films of Alfred Hitchcock) do not present an immediate connection to national security, especially with respect to the time of McCarthyism and the "Red Scare" in the America of the 1950s. Yet, Corber goes to tremendous effort to suggest that there is a more than substantial relationship. While reading these chapters, I do not fully expect you to understand the substance of his argument, but you should read the chapters with an eye to understanding HOW rhetorically he is making this relationship. So read with this intention:

- In "Draped in the American Flag", what does Corber say that Arthur Schlesinger does in his book, The Vital Center?
- In order to come to terms with Schlesinger, Corber also uses a work of Hannah Arendt. Why does he do this and what does he achieve in the end?

- In "Reconstructing Homosexuality," Corber is extremely intrigued by Hitchcock's Strangers on a Train. What is the basis of this interest/problem?
- What sources does Corber use to address this interest/problem and how does he do it?

Please come prepared to discuss these in class. As you have been doing in the last few weeks, please remember to print out a hard copy of the readings and work on that copy. Since the readings are fairly difficult, working on a hard copy can be especially helpful.
# Meeting 8A (Thinking with Writing: Danger and Security)

Source: course site lesson page, saved 7 Oct 2026. Links are as published on the page.

### Week 8: Meeting 8A
**Topical discussion**  
Oct 6, 2026

## Activities

- Discuss concept of “moral panic” via Stanley Cohen
- Group scenarios on the development of moral panics in Singapore

In this topical discussion session, we continue our focus on how danger is socially constructed through the formation of moral panics. As you will read in Cohen, a moral panic is “[a] condition, episode, person or group of persons [who emerge] to become defined as a threat to societal values and interests” (for explanation of transposals in the square brackets, see REF 12). No society is immune to them, but analysing them from an intellectual and critical perspective, we can see how paranoia develops, how different tools of society (like the mass media, social and community institutions) collaborate to amplify the panic, and how certain ingroups and outcasts are created. In brief, moral panics evoke fear, anxiety, dread, and moral judgement.

We have two goals for this session. One of them is to discuss one chapter from Cohen’s classic 1972 study on Folk Devils and Moral Panics, and to consider how we might employ his suggested framework. But the second brings us closer to home: how can we use Cohen to help us understand two points in Singapore’s history that brought us close to moral panics:

- The west-toxification discourse of the early 1970s, in which Singapore’s political leaders and institutions expressed deep anxiety over the encroachment of “decadent” western culture into Singapore like Hippyism, consumerism, and fashion.
- The era of the McDonald’s or Centrepoint kids in the mid-1980s, when increasingly large numbers of youths started to spend large amounts of time hanging out in shopping malls, thus sparking concerns of delinquency and criminality.

As a way of further taking things one step further, we will have small group work to imagine alternate scenarios of how the moral panic in these two events could have developed. For example, how could they have worsened? What would societal reactions look like? And how would the moral panic dissipate?

## Preparations
To prepare for this session, please read:

- Cohen, Stanley. Folk Devils and Moral Panics: The Creation of the Mods and Rockers. 3rd ed. Routledge, 1972/2011. Chapter 1, “Deviance and Moral Panics”, pp. 1-20. (This new edition has a new 40+ page introduction, which updates the ideas and approaches taken, but read this if you have the time. It’s an easy read but quite long). [[Download](https://www-taylorfrancis-com.libproxy1.nus.edu.sg/books/mono/10.4324/9780203828250/folk-devils-moral-panics-stanley-cohen)]

Then read/view the following materials to get a better understanding of the two events in Singapore:

West-toxification of the early 1970s

- Yew, Leong. Asianism and the Politics of Regional Consciousness in Singapore. Routledge, 2013. (Read pp. 88-90 from the section, “Asia in Singapore’s cultural crises” until the end of the first paragraph on p.90, which you will find in the chapter, “In search of the Asian soul”). This small reading will give you the historical background. [[Download](https://www-taylorfrancis-com.libproxy1.nus.edu.sg/books/mono/10.4324/9780203561881/asianism-politics-regional-consciousness-singapore-leong-yew)]
- “Danger of becoming a nation of Wogs: Dr Goh”. The Straits Times. December 11, 1972, pp. 1, 9. (This article starts on p. 1 and continues on p. 9. Make sure you read both pages) [[Link to p. 1](https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/digitised/article/straitstimes19721211-1.2.10)] [[Link to p. 9](https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/digitised/article/straitstimes19721211-1.2.41)]

Centrepoint kids of the mid-1980s

- Watch this video clip from the channel 5 current affairs programme, Feedback. [[Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdyZfxkpSFd/)]
- Read this newspaper article: Leong Weng Kam, “Centrepoint Kids must go, says youth group”. The Straits Times. January 28, 1986, p. 36. [[Download](https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/digitised/article/straitstimes19860128-1.2.73)]
# Meeting 8B (Thinking with Writing: Danger and Security)

Source: course site lesson page, saved 7 Oct 2026. Links are as published on the page.

### Week 8: Meeting 8B
**Paper 2 peer reviews**  
Oct 8, 2026

Venue: RC3-01-01

Since you have already done a peer review session in week 3, what we will do in this session should now be familiar to you. As in the previous peer review, this will be a chance for you to read and give comments for the work written by the other members of your peer review group, and for you to receive comments for your own writing. Still, please read the rest of the instructions carefully and take note of the group assignments and the documents that you must make use of.

## Your Tasks

- Please arrange, as soon as possible, with your group members how you would like to circulate your drafts. This can either be by email or a shared cloud folder, such as Google Docs or Microsoft OneDrive. Ensure your own paper is distributed by Wednesday, October 7, 6 pm (i.e. the evening before the peer review session). If you absolutely cannot make this time, you must make additional arrangements with your group so they know when to expect your work and still have enough time to read and comment on your paper.
- Before distributing your draft, please make sure that (a) the selected texts for your comparative analysis are included or you have provided instructions on how to access those texts; and (b) the you've [completed the self-appraisal form](https://dns.teachsystems.com/viewobj.cfm?id=1192)
(or alternatively form the docudex) and included it in your document.

- Please give yourself enough time before the peer review session to read and comment on the other papers. I would strongly suggest you look at the self-appraisal form after you read the paper, and then assess if the author's self-appraisal aligns with your own reading of their paper. Remember: there will not be enough time to start reading the papers in the peer review session itself. You must arrive already having done so.
- (Optional) Download and look through the paper 2 grading rubric below.

## Reading papers from your group
The process of doing this is similar to what you did in the first peer review session. As expected, you should read the papers critically, paying attention to aspects like textual selection, CMT, argumentation, and your overall "feel" of the paper. It's perfectly fine to let your emotions come in. How do you feel about it? Do you feel happy, satisfied? Confused or worried? These "affects" are crucial because they serve as the gateway for you to ask why this might be so and what aspects of that writing might have led you to feel that way. But because this is a different assignment, you should also pay attention to new requirements:

- The grounds for comparison and the frame of reference used in the selection of the two texts.
- The exposition of both texts and how this now make for a more sophisticated paper, as compared with the earlier single text close reading.

- The performance of the comparative or lens analysis.
- Argument structure (now that we've covered it more substantially)

## GROUP ASSIGNMENTS
AM Section

Group 1: Emma, Alex, Samuel, Zi Yue

Group 2: Joshua, Manae, Rahul, Ziheng

Group 3: Yixiang, Rei, Kai Li, Hongrui

PM Section

Group 1: Ian, Ashley, Isaac, Wayne

Group 2: Aidan, Si Xuan, An

Group 3: Athyna, Mona, Bethany, Fang Hong

## THINGS TO BRING

- Your laptop for screen sharing (and an HDMI adapter, if you have one)
- Obviously, notes you may have written for the papers you read

=== Possible texts/s10551-014-2075-1.pdf
J Bus Ethics DOI 10.1007/s10551-014-2075-1

Three-Level Mechanism of Consumer Digital Piracy: Development and Cross-Cultural Validation

Mateja Kos Koklic � Monika Kukar-Kinney � Irena Vida



Received: 8 June 2013 / Accepted: 21 January 2014 � Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2014



Abstract Digital piracy as a continuing problem significantly impacts various stakeholders, including consumers, enterprises, and countries. This study develops a threelevel mechanism of determinants of consumer digital piracy behavior, with personal risk as an individual factor, susceptibility to interpersonal influence as an inter-personal factor, and moral intensity as a broad societal factor. Further, it explores the role of rationalization and future piracy intent as outcomes of past piracy behaviors. The authors use survey data from four countries in the European Union to test the system of structural relationships. With an exception of the effect of consumers' susceptibility to interpersonal influence on piracy behavior, the conceptual model receives remarkably consistent support across the four countries. Specifically, perception of personal risk and moral intensity negatively affected the reported piracy behavior in all four countries. The results further support the negative influence of moral intensity and the positive influence of past digital piracy behavior on consumers' use of rationalization. Lastly, personal risk, rationalization, and past digital piracy behavior directly influenced consumers' intention to engage in digital piracy in the future. The study also discusses implications of the findings and identifies areas of future research.

M. Kos Koklic (&) � I. Vida Faculty of Economics, University of Ljubljana, Kardeljeva ploscad 17, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia e-mail: mateja.kos@ef.uni-lj.si

I. Vida e-mail: irena.vida@ef.uni-lj.si

M. Kukar-Kinney Robins School of Business, University of Richmond, Richmond, VA 23173, USA e-mail: mkukarki@richmond.edu



Keywords Digital piracy � Interpersonal influence � Moral intensity � Personal risk � Piracy intent � Rationalization

Introduction

Digital piracy, or consumer practice of illegally downloading files, such as music, movies, software, etc., from the Internet, represents a significant global threat to the welfare of industries producing digital products (Goode 2012; Taylor et al. 2009). Industry antipiracy group BASCAP (Business Action to Stop Counterfeiting and Piracy, 2011) estimates the worldwide income loss to range from $30 to $75 billion in digitally pirated music, movies, and software industries alone, rising up to $240 billion by 2015. In the European Union alone, the creative industries most impacted by piracy (i.e., recorded music, film, TV series, software) experienced retail revenue losses of close to 10 billion in 2008 due to piracy, largely in the digital domain. In addition, software piracy in the EU represents close to 4.5 billion in losses to the software industry in the EU over 1 year (TERA Consultants 2010). Another interesting aspect is highlighted by the percentage of European Internet users who visit unlicensed sites: the proportion of users who visited at least one such site was 27 % in November 2011 (IFPI--International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, 2012). A common assumption in such estimates is that consumers of pirated products would have bought the originals, had they not been available for free. Stylianou/ Western Criminology Review 11(2), 43-56 (2010)

Online citation: Stylianou, Stelios. 2010. "Victimless Deviance: Toward a Classification of Opposition Justifications." Western Criminology Review 11(2):43-56. (http://wcr.sonoma.edu/v11n2/Stylianou.pdf).



Victimless Deviance: Toward a Classification of Opposition Justifications

Stelios Stylianou University of Nicosia

Abstract: Attitudes toward victimless deviance, predominantly drug use and various sexual behaviors, are explored using data from forty-nine semi-structured in-depth interviews with participants from various social and cultural backgrounds. The central question addressed is why people oppose these behaviors. The study explores perceptions of the nature and the consequences of these behaviors and the normative principles based on which people form opinions of opposition. The results support that opposition to victimless deviance is structured based on three normative principles: the libertarian principle (opposing harm to others), the paternalistic principle (opposing harm to self), and the moralistic principle (opposing harmless wrongdoing). Arguments justifying these oppositions are presented in a classification of opposition justifications. Particular emphasis is given to moralistic oppositions.

Keywords: crime seriousness, victimless deviance, drug use, sexual deviance, libertarianism, paternalism, moralism, harm to others, harm to self, harmless wrongdoing



INTRODUCTION

Since its conception, victimless crime, and more inclusively, victimless deviance, has been a controversial issue in normative philosophy and criminal law. Various theses and arguments have emerged in an attempt to resolve a fundamental question regarding the limits of the law and more broadly social norms: should society control, through prohibition or other means, behaviors that do not harm others?1 The difficulty of this question is reflected in the debates on prohibition of victimless behaviors. Serious disagreements remain regarding "conflict crimes" or mala prohibita, i.e., criminalized behaviors that according to a substantial proportion of the population should be decriminalized. Different views regarding this matter are supported by arguments based on a number of distinct ideological orientations and on a spectrum of perceptions of the nature and consequences of the behaviors in question. In this respect, criminological research has not investigated victimless crime to a satisfactory degree. For example, why are people expected to "just say no" to drugs (both as potential users and as opinion holders)? Is it because of the perceived harmful consequences of drug



use, and if so, what are these consequences? Or is it because using drugs is "just wrong"? And then, what does this mean?

This study presents elements of the debate on the control of victimless behaviors at the level of individual opinion. It attempts to classify opposition justifications, i.e., arguments used to justify the disapproval of these behaviors. The research question addressed is why do people oppose victimless deviance such as drug use, sexual deviance, gambling, and other similar behaviors. The question focuses on the thinking involved in forming an opinion. The study does not address the etiology of opinion formation in the usual sense (i.e., identification of psychological and social correlates of attitudes).

PERCEPTIONS OF DEVIANCE AND NORMATIVE PRINCIPLESS

Paper 2: Paper Using Lens Analysis

As explained in the instructions for paper 2, a lens paper is something you write when you have discovered an issue or problem in one text, and can only do something to that issue or problem when you reference another text. This "doing" something includes (and is not limited only to) finding a solution, explaining, re-articulating, demonstrating, and contextualizing the issue or problem. To write a lens paper, you must realize that finding a primary and secondary text is a dynamic process. You must be willing to change either texts depending on the relevance of the material that you have found. So, if you think you've found your primary text but aren't able to find a suitable secondary text, you must be prepared to do one of a few things. You could change your primary text, secondary text, or the problem that you have identified in your primary text.



Sequentially, start by examining a probable primary text. As you have done in your earlier close reading paper, start by asking the same questions. What do you think the text obviously try to say to its readers and how? Can you find a non-obvious problem such as an irony, contradiction, or puzzle when you shift backwards and forwards between the text in general and its various minute details? The "problem" may not be a problem as such, but you could also identify things in the text that intensify or re-inforce the obvious message, but for some reason are not immediately noticeable. When you've identified your issue or problem, you must then start to ask yourself if the solution is "fully," "partially," or not evident in the text. If the latter categories of "partially" or "not" evident applies, then you are then on your way to finding the secondary text.



Locating the secondary text will probably be the most difficult thing to do, since "research" isn't something we will cover until unit 3. In any event, you must be able to condense your problem with the primary text in such a way that will help you locate the secondary text. Try a few keywords or key phrases like "terrorism," "war," "propaganda," and "social control." Use either an Internet search engine or the library's online catalogue (where you can search by keywords). Browse through the results, and if possible try to eliminate a few so that you have a workable set of possible secondary texts. From there onwards, there is no other way except for you to read the material to find one that suits you the most.



When you read the potential secondary text, you must constantly bear in mind the question that you've devised from the primary text. Find the key terms or ideas in the text. Does the main thesis of the secondary text provide the solution? Or are there more specific arguments, or just evidence that will help you? When this is found, you will then be ready to put your paper together.
=====
Paper 2: Paper Using Comparative Analysis

The idea behind comparative analyses is to allow you to make certain propositions that make more sense when they are derived collectively from a few texts. For the comparative paper then the idea is to find two texts that have some form of association. This association can be a common explicit message, object, colour, pattern, narrative, genre, and so on. The association should then be something that forms a problem, issue, or puzzle that becomes evident when both texts placed side by side. So basically, what you're doing here is a close reading exercise, but on two texts. Your motive will come from both texts, and your main claim (thesis) will have to be supported by evidence that comes from within one or both texts. As in the first paper, please don't let both texts be a platform for discussing general issues.====

Why #7 comes first


Stylianou sorts objections to victimless deviance into three types: harm to others, harm to self, and "harmless wrongdoing." The paper also notes that people who object often point to "psychological harm to others, particularly their loved ones," and that these "harm to others" arguments usually rest on "a confusion between the behavior itself and other elements."
That describes the Oct 2025 "Horrors of Vaping Are Real" triptych almost exactly:
  • Breaking Dad is about a father who lost his daughter.
  • Danger Things is about a friend who died at 17: "Help your friends quit."
  • Final Destination: ICU is about harm to the vaper themselves.

So there's a puzzle inside the text, which is the kind of motive the instructor wants. Vaping is a victimless offence, yet two of the three posters centre someone other than the vaper. A possible thesis: the posters move the harm of vaping from the self onto the vaper's family and friends, and "illegal" closes off any question of whether the harm is real. That's a claim about what the posters do, not about government intent.
It also answers a question the instructor raised themselves to the AM group: if liberal societies leave vaping to self-regulation because it harms no one else, why is Singapore so restrictive?
One risk: "The horrors of vaping are real" is the same campaign the AM "Stop Vaping" group presented, and the instructor has already commented on it. If you weren't in that group, consider the NUS posters as your primary text instead. "Friends Don't Let Friends Vape" and the line telling students to report vaping to Campus Security fit the same lens. If you were in that group, it falls under "texts you chose for your group homework," which also needs the instructor's OK.

One fix is to notice that Cohen's folk devils are people, while these posters make the device the devil and the vaper its victim. Since you can only use two texts, I'd hold Cohen for Paper 3.
  • #5: Keep everything the same except time: same country, same agencies, before and after the kpod/etomidate shift. Pair the Jan 2024 "toxic friend" poster with the Oct 2025 triptych. Don't use the 2023 MacPherson pledge poster, because its goal is getting people to a CC event, a different objective (the same problem the instructor flagged for the anti-drugs group). Drop "almost seems controlled." Your Google Trends chart works as context, not as the argument.

That links to the danger-and-security theme through cybersecurity, and you could still use Kos Koklic's "personal risk" and "moral intensity" as context.

3	 Defending Rohan, Fangorn and the Shire
4	 According to the Concise English Oxford Dictionary (Eleventh Edition), a
5	community can be defined as "a group of people living together in one place,
6	especially one practising common ownership" or "the people of an area or
7	country considered collectively". This collective spirit and commonality of a
8	community is exemplified in Peter Jackson's film, "The Lord of the Rings: The
9	Two Towers". An adaptation from J. R. R. Tolkien's novel by the same name,
10	the film illustrates how the inhabitants of various settlements, namely the
11	Elves, the Hobbits, the Men and the Ents (`shepherds of the trees'), cooperate to
12	defend their territory in Middle-earth against a common threat, symbolised by
13	the Isengard's tower of Orthanc and the Sauron's tower of Barad-dur (hence
14	`the Two Towers'). Apart from unilateral efforts to rally the support of their own
15	people, they also formed coalitions to resist the threat, for instance the
16	collaboration of the Elves and the people of Rohan during the battle at Helm's
17	Deep. Just as an individual would protect himself or herself as an innate
18	response to survival, it seems that this notion to defend oneself as well as
19	others in the same community as portrayed in the film is almost instinctive as
20	well. This is exemplified by the citizens of Rohan, who intuitively acknowledge
21	the importance of defending their country (as Aragorn pointed out, specifically
22	the `women and children') without explicitly questioning its rationale.
23	 This supposedly innate quality evident in "The Lord of the Rings: The Two
24	Towers" seems to be an apparent contradiction to Ernest Renan's essay, "What
25	is a Nation?", which implies that such sentiments are nurtured rather than
26	naturally determined. In his essay, Renan asserts that `a large aggregate of
27	men, healthy in mind and warm of heart, creates the kind of moral conscience
28	which we call a nation'. In other words, a nation is ultimately an imagined
29	community subject to interpretations by the people living in it. Relating these
30	definitions back to the film where similar ideas concerning a community are
31	also being explored, the reasons for which people defend their communities are
32	then better explained. Far from being intrinsic, people's sense of belonging
33	 1
34	towards a place was only internalised much later, when different individuals
35	could identify with common elements demarcated by the `community'. It is thus
36	with this common attachment to their land in mind that they fight on behalf of
37	the other people in the same community. Hence, using Renan's concept of a
38	nation to demonstrate how a community could possibly operate, this essay
39	argues that the notion of defending one's homeland, a theme recurrent
40	throughout the film "The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers", is fundamentally
41	different from the idea of protecting oneself, in that the former stems from one's
42	affiliation with the community while the latter is believed to be an inborn trait.
43	 "The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers" conveys the themes of
44	sovereignty, threats and defence through a public symbol of danger: Sauron. He
45	has plans to destroy Middle-earth, which clearly pose a threat to the existence
46	of the various communities since there is a conflict over territorial space. On
47	one hand, he instigates Saruman, the White Wizard, to attack the land of
48	Rohan; on the other, he himself `turned his eye to Gondor' (quite literally). To
49	overcome these threats, the communities had come up with various defence
50	tactics. In doing so, what were they trying to protect? Renan explains that `to
51	have performed great deeds together, to wish to perform still more - these are
52	the essential conditions for being a people'. In the case of Rohan, it was believed
53	that protecting the `legacy of memories' in the past, manifested in the form of
54	national symbols such as the castle at Edoras and the supposedly impregnable
55	fortress at Helm's Deep, would help in instilling a common faith. Though the
56	country of Rohan was facing imminent peril, King Theoden asserted his claim
57	over the land by insisting that it was "not a defeat; [the people of Rohan] will
58	return" to occupy the land once more. His preoccupation with the physical
59	territory and determination to preserve the sovereignty of their country shows
60	his ambition to continue the `legacy' passed down from predecessors, which
61	further proves the `will to perpetuate the value of the heritage' in the present.
62	Renan also asserts that people of a nation will share `common glories in the
63	past' and `a common will in the present'. This is in line with the behaviour of
64	the Hobbits, who have, on more than one occasion, mentioned their affiliation
65	with the Shire and the desire to return to their homeland because they want to
66	protect whatever was handed down from their predecessors (in Frodo's case,
67	 2
68	Bilbo) and carry on the legacy. These examples show that as opposed to the
69	individual who is perhaps more preoccupied with his or her personal safety,
70	community interests centre on the protection of past values, preservation of the
71	present way of life and paving the way for future generations. This emphasis on
72	continuity can perhaps be attributed to the significance of commonality in
73	building a community, such that shared experiences and codes help to
74	strengthen one's attachment to the community.
75	 The use of phrases such as `common customs posts and frontiers' as well
76	as `having suffered, enjoyed, and hoped together' in Renan's essay give
77	emphasis to the importance of having shared experiences, from which a
78	common value system may develop. Fighting for the common good of the
79	community should thus be a logical extension of this idea. During the battle at
80	Helm's Deep, for example, citizens of Rohan valiantly fought to protect their
81	own territory under the leadership of King Theoden. This very notion of
82	defending one's country, however, is something we have always taken for
83	granted: it seems that we seldom question ourselves why national loyalty would
84	necessitate the laying down of lives. Consider then the scenes depicting pre-war
85	sentiments reflected by the citizens of Rohan. Interestingly, apart from
86	illustrating military preparations for the battles, Jackson chooses to focus on
87	civilian reactions to warfare as well. If community defence is merely the
88	aggregation of individual responses to survival, then women and children ill-
89	equipped with methods of warfare will be expected to defend themselves on
90	their own. This is certainly not the case in the film, where soldiers (identified by
91	the ability to wield swords) fight their enemies on behalf of the weaker ones in
92	society. Hence, bringing attention to the faces of helpless women and
93	defenceless children leads us to question the soldiers' motivation in defending
94	others in the same community.
95	 To clarify this, a critical analysis of Renan's ideas about sacrifice and
96	suffering is imperative. He argues that `suffering in common unifies more than
97	joy does' and that `griefs are thus of more value than triumphs'. In particular,
98	since the nation is the `culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice, and
99	devotion', and the notion of sacrifice implies that one has taken others' interests
100	into consideration, this thus helps to explain why people are willing to fight for
101	 3
102	common ideals as opposed to personal interests. As such one can gain a better
103	understanding why, in the film, Aragorn makes a plea with King Theoden of
104	Rohan to `defend the women and children': it is because women and children
105	are seen to be incapable of defending themselves, and so this warrants the help
106	of soldiers who are willing to sacrifice their lives in return. Defending the
107	community, then, may not involve the mobilisation of all citizens, for there exist
108	able-bodied representatives who are willing to sacrifice for others on the basis of
109	having a common faith.
110	 Despite the efforts of individual communities to demarcate and protect
111	the areas bound by their territory, the borders of such settlements are
112	ultimately not impervious to external influences. As seen in "The Lord of the
113	Rings: The Two Towers", the Ents were relatively unperturbed by the external
114	events happening in Middle-earth, and claimed that `this [was] not [their] war';
115	for instance they were indifferent towards the impending attacks of the Urukhai
116	army on Rohan, though Merry and Pippin the Hobbits tried to convince them
117	that they were `part of the world' as well. It was only when the Urukhais had
118	infringed their territorial rights to the forest and caused destruction to trees
119	(friends they have `known from nut and acorn') that the Ents decided to
120	retaliate. In addition, the majority of the Elves had plans to abandon Middle-
121	earth for the journey `into the West', in favour of their preference for immortality
122	over the well being of Middle-earth. However, Galadriel, the Elven Queen,
123	cautioned that `the time of the Elves [will be] over when all of Middle-earth is
124	destroyed'. This corresponds with Renan's assertion that `nations participate in
125	the common work of civilisation'. Because of the inter-relatedness of each
126	community and the rest of Middle-earth, these communities cannot be merely
127	seen as independent entities on their own. This means that apart from
128	identifying the Ents, the Men, the Elves and the Hobbits as four distinct and
129	separate communities, there is a need to consider the larger community
130	consisting of every being in Middle-earth to deal with threats that cannot be
131	resolved unilaterally. The existence of overlapping communities as such then
132	suggests that a person may concurrently adopt multiple identities within
133	several communities, to "sound the great note of humanity". When people are
134	more aware of the larger space they belong to, they are also more likely to
135	 4
136	appreciate what previously seemed like remote issues. This thus explains the
137	Elves' and the Ents' eventual decision to stay and help Middle-earth, something
138	that would not have been achieved if each individual was only concerned about
139	his or her personal sphere of influence.
140	 Prior to declaring war on Rohan, Saruman the White Wizard proclaimed
141	that "there will be no dawn for men". Such times of pessimism invoke in people
142	the need to preserve sovereignty and ensure sustenance of their own
143	communities, since `one loves in proportion of the sacrifices to which one has
144	consented, and in proportion to the ills that one has suffered'. Apart from a
145	need to defend the community's historical heritage and contemporary culture, it
146	is also critical to instil a common faith in its people, which can be shaped by
147	shared experiences. It is thus the combination of the above-mentioned two
148	factors that necessitates defending the community as a whole rather than as
149	individuals.
150	 That said, this essay does not assume that the countries or communities
151	featured in Jackson's film can be equated with `nations', a very complex issue
152	on its own. Rather, this essay seeks to highlight the similarities between such a
153	fictitious representation and a theorist's interpretation, from which one can
154	perhaps gain a better understanding of the `community'. Nations, just like any
155	other community, are but man-made entities. Though the creation of an
156	identity is crucial for a community to survive, one must not forget that such an
157	identity has to be created by its inhabitants in the first place. In emphasising
158	the elements of a community, therefore, it would be useful to discuss the role of
159	the individuals in dictating and forging these very elements as well.
