187	 National or Global?
188	 In recent years, national security has become an important and pressing issue for
189	the United States of America (USA). Since the realization that enemies can penetrate the
190	country's defenses and strike at the heart of major cities as they had done in the
191	September 11 attacks five years ago, the self-proclaimed beacon of freedom of the world
192	was now imprisoned in a shroud of fear. President George W. Bush declared that this act
193	of terror was an attack against USA's freedom. A new national security strategy was
194	required to deal with new threats in the new security environment and new national
195	security strategies, such as The National Security Strategy of the United States of
196	America, 2002, were drawn up by the White House. The purpose of a National Security
197	Strategy is to highlight the government's plan to protect a country against the threats to
198	their freedom. However, this is not evident in the preface of The National Security
199	Strategy of the United States of America, 2002, written by President George W. Bush.
200	One would expect the National Security Strategy to focus on how the government of the
201	USA will protect the country from threats to its freedom; however, the document focuses
202	more on how it can help protect the freedom of the world from what the USA perceives
203	as threats rather than its own internal security. This perspective is underscored by a close
204	reading of the preface of the national security policy of Canada. This paper shows how
205	the preface to the National Security Strategy of the USA positions it as a global security
206	strategy which the USA sees itself as leading.
207	 In the preface, the USA, represented by its leader the President, appears to speak
208	for everyone by universalizing its concerns and positions on various global issues. It
209	positions itself as the voice of all humanity articulating concerns on behalf of all nations.

214	claiming to know what everyone in the world wants and trying to highlight the duties of

216	National Security Strategy of the USA is no longer meant for an American audience but

218	security of the United States but more on what the world needs to secure, which,
219	according to the preface, is its freedom.

378	Rhetorically, your paper shows a good attempt at performing a lens analysis. There is a
379	sense of how to develop or identify a problem within a particular text, and how to find
380	some sort of resolution (through a type inductive reasoning) in another text. It is clearly
381	written and the reader can follow your train of thought.
382	However, there are quite a few issues concerning structure, organization, and reasoning
383	that you will need to address to make your paper more compelling:
384	 1. In your introduction, the contextualizing statement is somewhat generic. Wouldn't it be
385	 better to point out a general characteristics of national security policies for which the U.S.
386	 could then be described as an exception? This is important because if you later use
387	 Canada as a counter-example, there is no basis for your reader to figure out which is the
388	 norm and which is the exception.
389	 2. Connected to point 1, I can't understand why Canada's national security policy preface
390	 has been used as a lens text. This needs more explanation/rationalization.
391	 3. While it is important to further explain the "problem", which you have done over four
392	 pages, the discussion here has been somewhat disorganized. It looks like you are doing a
393	 point-by-point commentary on how U.S. national security policy doesn't sound like a
394	 regular national security policy. The last paragraph in the section is most central to this,
395	 so it might be better to have it way in front and the other paragraphs reorganized and

84	Power in Propaganda: Examining Depictions of Gender and Power Relations in State
85	 Propaganda during World War II
86	 During World War II (WWII), state propaganda in Western countries often invoked
87	patriarchal gender stereotypes when depicting power relations between men and women. Men
88	were predominantly portrayed in positions of power over women, especially in campaigns
89	encouraging men to play more active roles in the war effort. For instance, wartime posters
90	urging men to volunteer for military service featured Japanese soldiers inflicting violence on
91	female victims. These used the stereotype of women as weak and powerless, and men as their
92	stronger protectors, to demonise the enemy and encourage male participation in warfare. Both
93	chosen texts originated in such a historical and cultural context, being WWII government
94	propaganda posters published in Western nations to persuade men to fulfill wartime
95	responsibilities. "Keep Mum She's Not So Dumb" was published in 1942 by the Ministry of
96	Information in Britain, as part of the "Careless Talk" campaigns which cautioned soldiers
97	against accidentally divulging information to the enemy. It features the image of a woman
98	with three conversing military officers, with a caption that reads "Keep mum she's not so
99	dumb! Careless talk costs lives". The poster implies that men should be careful of their
100	speech around women, who may pass information to the enemy. "He Volunteered for
101	Submarine Service" was published in 1944 by the United States Office of War Information. It
102	depicts a woman embracing a sailor from the military. It aims to encourage men to volunteer
103	for submarine service by suggesting that doing so will make men attractive to women.
104	 Given the provenance of the texts and the trends observed in texts of similar origin,
105	one might expect the texts' portrayals of men and women to feature the traditional power
106	 3
107	dynamic of men possessing power over women. However, the texts do not portray power
108	relations in this clear-cut manner, instead depicting complex power dynamics between men,
109	women and a third party -- the narrator. In both texts, the narrator seems to be the respective
110	government agency responsible for producing each text. In "Keep Mum", both the woman in
111	the text and the narrator undermine men's intelligence, treating them as gullible to women's
112	schemes. Yet, the narrator describes women as "not so dumb" -- a backhanded compliment
113	that underestimates women -- and undermines women's moral character by villainising
114	them. In "He Volunteered", the woman's actions and narrator's words seem to undermine
115	men by predicating their worth on membership in the military. Yet, the text can also be
116	viewed as objectifying women by portraying them as a soldier's "prize", and empowering
117	men by endowing them with an honorable patriotic duty.
118	 I argue that the complexity of power relations between the three actors maximises the
119	effectiveness of both texts in achieving their purposes. By striking a balance between
120	undermining and empowering men, the texts persuade their male target audiences to act as
121	they suggest. This can be observed from examining three layers of textual relationships:
122	between men and woman, men and narrator, and woman and narrator. Both the woman and
123	narrator undermine men -- male characters in the text and male viewers of the text
124	respectively -- to convince viewers of a problem they must act to resolve. Yet, the narrator
125	also undermines women in a way that further encourages the viewer to take action.
126	 Both texts reverse the conventional relationship of men having power over women.
127	Instead, in the texts, the woman possesses power over men by being the object of their desire.
128	Meanwhile, she covets something the men have but does not sincerely reciprocate their
129	attraction -- she uses her relationship with men for her personal gain. The power asymmetry
130	in their relationship arises from the men's seeming obliviousness to her ulterior motives. This
131	power dynamic is central to both texts achieving their purposes: it sets up a problem scenario
132	in each text's narrative, which requires men to resolve in a certain manner. In "Keep Mum",
133	the men are attracted to the woman. She poses seductively on the couch, wearing a
134	form-fitting gown and adorned with jewellery. While the three men converse with one
135	another, their body language demonstrates their interest towards her. They are leaning
136	downwards, positioning their bodies to face her or be closer to her. Two of the men have her
137	in their line of sight; while the third looks away from her, his hand rests possessively on her
138	arm, perhaps indicating that she is his date. Interestingly, the woman faces away from them.
139	 4
140	A power imbalance can be observed: while the men are enamoured with the woman, she
141	outwardly pays them no mind and effortlessly retains their attention. The visual composition
142	of the poster also reflects this power imbalance. The woman is situated front and centre,
143	occupying the viewer's attention, while the men are merely in the background. The situation
144	is problematised by the text's caption, which implies that the woman may be an enemy spy
145	eavesdropping on the men's conversation for information. The men, blinded by their
146	attraction to her, are oblivious to her machinations. Hence, the woman is able to use her
147	power over men for her personal gain, to the detriment of the men and war effort. In "He
148	Volunteered", a beautiful woman embraces a soldier while he gazes at her with a smile.
149	However, she does not mirror his gaze. Her eyes are trained admiringly on a military badge
150	pinned on his uniform, which she strokes with her hand. It seems that she does not sincerely
151	reciprocate his affections -- what truly interests her is his membership in the military. The
152	edges of the man's image even appears to dissolve into the background, as if he is fading into
153	insignificance. Similar to "Keep Mum", there is a power imbalance in their relationship in the
154	woman's favour: while the man seems infatuated with the woman, she is merely fixated on
155	his occupation, not him. While this power dynamic is not portrayed as a danger to national
156	security (as it is in "Keep Mum"), the text poses it as a problem to men, implying that a man
157	has to attain a certain career or status to win over a woman. Thus, both texts depict an
158	unconventional power dynamic whereby men are undermined by women. This forms the
159	basis of a problem presented by each text, which the male viewer is compelled to resolve.
160	 Men are not only undermined in the relationship between male and female characters
161	within the texts, but also in the relationship between the narrator and male viewers of the text.
162	The narrator acts as a voice of authority or judgement. Through the texts' captions, the
163	narrators question whether the viewer possesses ideal male qualities like intelligence and
164	attractiveness. By striking a blow to the male ego, the narrator compels the viewer to
165	undertake the action recommended by the text, which presumably will allow him to reassert
166	his masculinity. In "Keep Mum", the narrator warns male soldiers: "Keep mum she's not so
167	dumb! Careless talk costs lives". This not only proclaims women are more intelligent than
168	commonly thought, but also undermines men's intelligence by suggesting men are gullible to
169	women's deception. The narrator's tone is chiding, mimicking a figure of authority scolding a
170	subordinate -- undermining the male viewer's status. The imagery in the text supports this
171	message. From the appearance of their uniforms, the three men are military officers
172	representing the three branches of the British Armed Forces. Their obliviousness to the
173	 5
174	female spy implies that even experienced soldiers from all backgrounds can easily fall prey to
175	a woman. Furthermore, the text utilises the illustration of the woman to challenge the male
176	viewer. Unlike the men, the woman confidently makes direct eye contact with the viewer
177	with a small grin, as if taunting him about her successful scheming. Considering that women
178	were usually portrayed as more passive characters (compared to men) in the media, this is
179	likely a deliberate choice by the text's designer to emphasise the narrator's message. By
180	undermining men, especially their intelligence -- which was then-considered a masculine
181	trait -- the narrator damages the male ego. Hence, the viewer feels compelled to reassert
182	himself by proving the narrator wrong, which fulfills the text's aim. In "He Volunteered", the
183	narrator attributes the woman's interest in the man to the fact that "He Volunteered for
184	Submarine Service". This implies that a man's attractiveness depends on him joining the
185	military. More than that, viewed with the text's imagery, the narrator's words tie masculinity
186	itself to military service. The soldier's physical appearance embodies many traditional facets
187	of masculinity, especially juxtaposed against the woman's femininity. He appears strong and
188	capable in his uniform, and his tan complexion is evidence of hard labour. He is also
189	accompanied by a beautiful woman -- which some would consider a male achievement, as
190	his smirk suggests. By illustrating the soldier to be a paragon of masculinity, the text makes
191	him the ideal that young men should aspire to: to be a man is to be a soldier. The narrator's
192	words implicitly challenge the viewer's own maleness -- if he has not volunteered, his
193	masculinity is diminished. Thus, by undermining men, and associating masculinity with a
194	certain behaviour, the narrator in each text compels the male viewer to act as the text
195	suggests.
196	 However, the relationship between the narrator and women seems to tell a different
197	story. The narrator undermines women in both texts, albeit in varying ways. By doing so, the
198	narrator conversely reinvests men with some power. Thus, the texts perform a delicate
199	balancing act. They undermine men to elicit certain reactions from the male viewer, on the
200	basis that he will want to reassert his masculinity. On the other hand, they empower men to a
201	limited extent -- sufficient to further encourage the viewer to take action. In "Keep Mum",
202	the woman's intelligence is undermined by the narrator's condescending comment that she's
203	"not so dumb" -- a backhanded compliment that implies women are, in fact, still somewhat
204	dumb. This seems to be a concession to reassure male viewers that it is not too difficult to foil
205	a woman's schemes, as long as they are careful. The narrator also villainises women, offering
206	an oversimplistic generalisation of women as possible enemy spies. By suggesting that any
207	 6
208	woman could be a threat, the text ensures viewers will be careful at all times. It also places
209	viewers on a moral high ground, giving them a moral responsibility to keep mum. In "He
210	Volunteered", while the woman can be viewed as asserting her power over the man, the
211	narrator can also be viewed as undermining the woman by objectifying her. In the illustration,
212	the red stripes on the woman's blouse, along with the stars around the caption, resemble the
213	red stripes and stars on the American flag. This imagery suggests that volunteering for
214	military service is a matter of patriotic duty. Judging from the woman's attire, her patriotism
215	makes her grateful towards the soldier, which presents a romantic opportunity he takes
216	advantage of. In this light, the narrator seems to use women as "bait" to entice men to join the
217	military, characterising them as potential rewards for men who volunteer. The narrator
218	presents men with the chance to play the hero and win the girl -- both traditional hallmarks
219	of masculinity. While "He Volunteered" at first inflicts a crisis of masculinity on the male
220	viewer, it also offers a solution that can empower him. Thus, in both texts, the complex
221	power relations between men, women and narrator coalesce to elicit the texts' desired
222	behaviours from their male target audiences.
223	 Both texts skilfully utilise complex depictions of gender and power relations to
224	achieve their purposes. However, they may be limited by the assumptions their strategy is
225	based upon -- chiefly the assumption that men are primarily motivated by a need to conform
226	to conventional standards of masculinity. Other assumptions include viewers' acceptance of
227	gender stereotypes, and the susceptibility of viewers' self-perception to external influences.
228	Nevertheless, the texts were likely quite effective during the time period of WWII, when
229	progressive ideas about gender were less mainstream and there was greater societal pressure
230	to conform to traditional gender norms.

239	Name
240	Module Number/ Tutorial Group UWC2101S/ Section 2

243	Date of submission 15/3/2007
244	Number of words 2200
245	 After the first successful test of a Soviet nuclear weapon in 1949, atomic bombs wielded by a
246	communist Soviet Union became an unprecedented threat to the safety of American civilians. Civil
247	defence authorities were tasked to prepare the American civilian population for all-out nuclear war
248	through various methods such as the construction of public fallout shelters and public education. "Duck
249	and Cover" was an educational film released in 1952 by the Federal Civil Defense Administration
250	(FCDA) to educate Americans that "ducking and covering" under tables and besides walls will protect
251	them from the worst effects of an atomic blast. It appears to have been an educational film designed to be
252	shown to schoolchildren by teachers in a classroom environment.
253	 Nearly fifty years later, Michael Moore referenced "Duck and Cover" on a segment of his
254	television programme "The Awful Truth". Pakistan and India had both successfully tested atomic
255	weapons and Moore saw an analogy in the relationship between the two rival countries and the
256	relationship between the United States and the Soviet Union in the early years of the Cold War, when
257	"Duck and Cover" was released. He placed himself in the role of a teacher to a classroom of Pakistani and
258	Indian adult students sitting on undersized tables and chairs, showing his students "Duck and Cover" and
259	interpreting its lessons for them - just as a schoolteacher in the 1950s might conceivably have done - and
260	filmed their reactions for comic effect. For the (presumably) adult American audience, humour could be
261	derived from parallels between the experience of the Pakistani and Indian adults and their own experience
262	as schoolchildren in the Cold War learning "Duck and Cover".
263	 There might appear to be little grounds for comparison between these two films - "Duck and
264	Cover" is a public educational film released in 1952, while this particular segment of "The Awful Truth"
265	is a satire released in the late 90s that incorporated elements of "Duck and Cover". However, they share
266	something in common in that two types of relationships are present in both films - teacher-student and
267	adult-child. What is more, closer inspection reveals that the identities of the parties playing each of the
268	roles are fluid and mutable - in "Duck and Cover", the identities of "teacher" and "adult" seem to be
269	interchangeable while in "The Awful Truth", the Pakistani and Indian adults seem to be taking on the
270	behaviour characteristics of children; In both films, the identities of the parties taking part in as well as
271	the boundaries between the relationships themselves are blurred.
272	 Therefore, this essay will argue that both films showcase a misalignment of the teacher-student
273	relationship with the adult-child relationship. This is because of the deep interconnections between the
274	discourse surrounding the teacher-student relationship and the discourse surrounding the adult-child
275	relationship.
276	 The respective discourses surrounding the two relationships inscribe the two relationships with
277	meaning, and the discourses are similar in that in both of them, the holders of power - teachers and adults
278	- wield an unchallenged amount of influence over the subjects of power - students and children. These
279	two discourses are different in that a teacher holds power because of extrinsic attributes - his job and his
280	knowledge (compared to students) - while an adult holds power because of intrinsic attributes - his age
281	and his physical prowess (compared to children). However, they are interconnected and confused simply
282	because teachers are usually adults and students are usually children. Because of the interlinks in the
283	discourses surrounding them, misalignment between the teacher-student relationship and the adult-child
284	relationship can occur where the party in the role of "teacher" is cast in the role of "adult" as well, while
285	the party in the role of "student" is forced to adopt the additional role of "child". This is what happens in
286	the relationships set up by both "Duck and Cover" and "The Awful Truth". The dual roles caused by this
287	misalignment allow the holder of power, the teacher/adult, to exert influence both within the boundaries
288	of the teacher-student discourse and the boundaries of the adult-child discourse on the subject of power,
289	the student/child, thus allowing the holder of power a disproportionate influence over the subject of
290	power.
291	 The misalignment that exists between the teacher-student relationship and the adult-child
292	relationship can be seen clearly within "The Awful Truth". Here, the parties playing the roles of "student"
293	and "teacher" are first established clearly by the classroom environment- the Pakistani and Indian adults
294	are "students" sitting in a classroom learning how to "duck and cover", while Moore is the "teacher"
295	standing in front of the class teaching them how to survive an atomic attack. The Pakistani and Indian
296	"students" are adults in the objective sense, yet their behaviour is more reminiscent of children than
297	adults. In particular, their immature attacks on each others' countries in the course of their squabbling -
298	such as "If Pakistan becomes number one, than India would be first number one!" - seem to be more
299	characteristic of small children than mature adults. This is interesting, because it suggests that the
300	environment surrounding them as "students", sitting on undersized tables in a cramped classroom, has
301	induced them to adopt the role of "children" as well.
302	 It might seem that this misalignment would resolve once out of the classroom; the "students"
303	should be less easily swayed outside the artificial environment of the classroom since they are adults as
304	well -and the discourses surrounding adult-adult relationships are usually discourses in which power is
305	more evenly spread out. However, this is not the case. Moore and another "teacher" he introduces later,
306	survival expert Chris Haggerty, have tremendous power and influence over the "students" even outside
307	the classroom. It appears that by claiming the role of "teacher", Moore and Haggerty subtly claim the
308	concurrent role of "adult", while the "students" subconsciously take on the role of "children" in response.
309	Because of this, the two of them are able to influence the "students" within the boundaries of both the
310	teacher-student and the adult-child discourse.
311	 This can perhaps best be seen when the "advanced students" are led on a "field trip" by Moore to
312	visit a fallout shelter maintained by Haggerty. The "students" embrace his survivalist rhetoric with
313	disturbing ease. They seem open to his ideas of putting family members suffering from radiation sickness
314	"out of their misery" and using their bodies as "protein sources" for survival. When he tells the students
315	that "your cousin comes knocking on that door and tries to get in here, you're going have to kill him.",
316	they seem to have been influenced by his dubious moral compass and respond enthusiastically like
317	children eager to please with responses in the same vein, such as "of course killing your cousin is not a
318	moral course, but in this case, we do not follow that rule because at this point, the cousin is already dead."
319	 Of course, "The Awful Truth" being a satire, there is a possibility that some of the Pakistani and
320	Indian citizens as well as Chris Haggerty were paid actors and that footage was purposely edited to distort
321	the truth for comic effect. However, these possibilities were both disregarded as there is no practical way
322	to affirm or deny them within the context of the two sources used for this essay.
323	 In "Duck and Cover", the misalignment between the teacher-student and adult-child relationships
324	is slightly more complex. This is because in addition to the teacher-student and adult-child relationships
325	formed within "Duck and Cover" itself, there is another teacher-student relationship present, between the
326	film itself, voiced by the narrator, and the viewer.
327	 Some explanation may be warranted here. Why would a viewer of "Duck and Cover", in
328	particular an adult viewer, in the 1950s be adopting the "student" role? After all, the adults depicted in
329	"Duck and Cover" itself seem to already know exactly what to do in the event of a nuclear attack.
330	However, since it is an educational film overtly designed to be shown to students, the viewer, whether
331	adult or child, is naturally prompted to take on the role of a "student" when watching this film. What is
332	more, "Duck and Cover" was released a mere three years after the first successful test of a Soviet nuclear
333	device. Thus, it was not unlikely that adults at the time were as ignorant of atomic war as portrayed in
334	"Duck and Cover" as children.
335	 This is not to say that "Duck and Cover" was not primarily aimed at schoolchildren, but "Duck
336	and Cover" was in the public domain after all, and it is probable that it was released with the secondary
337	purpose of educating these viewers in mind.
338	 Let us first examine the misalignment between the teacher-student and the adult-child
339	relationships within "Duck and Cover" itself. As mentioned above, the identities of "teacher" and "adults"
340	are referred to interchangeably, while the identities of "student" and "child" are conflated as well. For the
341	most part, relationships seem to be aligned quite well - "children" are always "students" and vice versa
342	while "teachers" are always "adults". However, "adults" are not always "teachers" in "Duck and Cover" -
343	they can be civil defence volunteers, housewives, or even strangers on the street. Yet in many ways,
344	"adults" serve the role of "teachers" as well: a civil defence volunteer "teaches" "Tony" when it is safe to
345	get up after an atomic bomb has exploded, while a stranger on the street "teaches" a young girl the
346	location of the nearest public shelter. This subtle misalignment of "teacher" with "adult" sets up a much
347	more serious misalignment in the relationship between "Duck and Cover" and its potential adult viewers.
348	 For reasons stated above, adult viewers are already likely to watch the film and relate to it as
349	"students". The portrayal of the "adults" in the film complicates this situation, since the adult viewers of
350	the film would probably be watching it for educational purposes and would not be able to identify with
351	the knowledgeable and powerful "adults" shown in "Duck and Cover". This portrayal of "adults" in
352	"Duck and Cover" thus encourages its adult viewers to dissociate themselves from their "adult" identity
353	and take on a "child" role instead.
354	 The narrator also contributes to the complication of misalignment of the teacher-student and
355	adult-child relationships caused by "Duck and Cover". He plays dual roles. On one hand, as the voice of
356	the educational film he fulfils the role of the "teacher" in the teacher-student relationship between the film
357	and the viewer. On the other hand, he plays a part in persuading adult viewers to take on the role of
358	"children". This is done very subtly. The narrator, with his deep and gruff voice, is undoubtedly a male
359	adult. Yet, he constantly identifies himself and the viewer with the "children" onscreen with lines such as
360	"we must get ready for it, just as we are ready for many other dangers that are around us all the time" and
361	"getting ready means we will all have to be able to take care of ourselves" (emphasis mine). This might
362	persuade the adult viewer to identify with the "children" depicted and take on the role of "child", just as
363	the narrator seems to do.
364	 The viewer is further encouraged to adopt the "child" role by "Duck and Cover" with the use of
365	the "Duck and Cover" song sung in the opening animated sequence. The repetition of words and the
366	simple tune encourage adult viewers to regress to a child-like state. This can be illustrated by the reaction
367	of the Pakistani ambassador in "The Awful Truth" upon viewing the opening sequence of "Duck and
368	Cover" - he sings the "Duck and Cover" song along with Moore and follows Moore's actions to the
369	music, just like a "child" instead of a dignified ambassador.
370	 In these ways, the viewer of "Duck and Cover", be he adult or child, is convinced to take on the
371	concurrent roles of "student" and "child". If the misalignment of the teacher-student and adult-child
372	relationships that can be seen within both "The Awful Truth" and "Duck and Cover" holds, it is likely
373	that "Duck and Cover" which is already in the role of "teacher" will assume the role of "adult" as well.
374	This brings us to our final question. Can a film play the role of an "adult" or a "teacher" by itself? Who
375	speaks through "Duck and Cover"? It would appear to be the FCDA, which commissioned the film. As
376	we have seen above, manipulating the misalignment between the teacher-student and adult-child
377	relationships gave Moore huge influence over his "students" in "The Awful Truth". Beyond its
378	educational purposes, was "Duck and Cover" also an attempt by the civil defence authorities to influence
379	the public to buy into civil defence rhetoric by utilising the misalignment between the teacher-student and
380	adult-child relationships?
381	 The answer to that question would be beyond the scope of this essay. What this essay has done is
382	to illustrate the misalignment between the teacher-student and adult-child relationships within both "The
383	Awful Truth" and "Duck and Cover" and postulate an additional misalignment in the teacher-student and
384	adult-child relationships between "Duck and Cover" and its adult viewers. This misalignment is present
385	because of interconnections in the discourse surrounding the two relationships and is present in films
386	from genres as diverse as education and satire.
387	Sources:
388	"Duck and Cover" Federal Civil Defense Administration and Archer Productions, Inc 1952
389	"The Awful Truth", segment on "Duck and Cover", Michael Moore

1	######## Sample_Paper_2_Significance_of_Government_Involvement_in_Emergencies_(no_comment.txt
2	 Paper 2: Comparative Analysis
3	 Significance of Government Involvement in Emergencies
4	 In a world, post September 11th 2001, countries face similar threats and have risen
5	to address them with many public readiness campaigns. Take for example the `Ready
6	.gov' and `Ready Singapore' websites created by the US Department of Homeland
7	Security and the Ministry of Home Affairs Singapore respectively. Both these websites
8	are directed to towards the mass public as a source of information and important
9	preparation details to boost the readiness of the citizens in the event of an emergency.
10	 These websites gives citizens of each country a clear idea of the level of
11	preparation expected and suggested steps to be taken to respond effectively to a threat.
12	Normally in an emergency, one would expect that in both countries, there would be
13	similar levels of citizen involvement in preparing for the threat and when the threat is
14	realised, the response to the threat should be composed of similarly. However when we
15	look at these two websites, the impression we get is not so. The Ready Singapore website
16	suggests rather minimal citizen involvement in comparison to America's Ready.gov
17	which actively encourages high level of planning and preparation. When we look at these
18	two websites together, a conflict is created whereby citizen preparation and participation
19	to respond the threat varies between the two countries facing similar threats.
20	 The role played by governments of each country is a key factor one must consider
21	when appreciating this conflict in citizen participation. Governments in both countries
22	play a major role in deciding and directing the responses of the citizens. The level of
23	government involvement will have a substantial effect on the level of citizen involvement
24	in a response to any threat. In this essay I will illustrate the conflict in expected citizen
25	participation rates and examine the significance of government participation that creates
26	this conflict.
27	 The most basic thing one is expected to do during an emergency is evacuate. Both
28	websites have addressed this issue with great importance ensuring that each of their
29	potential readers have a good idea of how to evacuate. Although most details are referred
30	to a Singapore Police Force website, Singapore's evacuation details are succinctly placed
31	under civil defence measures frequently asked questions as well. When asked where one
32	 Page 1 of 6
33	would evacuate to, the answer is "There will be evacuation marshals to direct you.
34	Follow the directions given by them..." The authoritative tone in this phrase signifies a
35	lack of decision making and involvement by the citizens and portrays that authorities are
36	actively involved in evacuation attempts and all the citizens need to do is simply `follow'
37	orders. In fact, such a statement could even suggest or lead to complacency by citizens
38	since they would solely rely on government's efforts and `follow' orders. In comparison
39	Ready America leaves the decision to evacuate up to the citizen. The evacuation details
40	or suggestions rather, are presented under the `Deciding to stay or go" title under the
41	"Make a plan" section. The words used in the title present the reader with a choice and
42	this connotation is repeated in the following paragraph when we read "Depending on
43	your circumstances and the nature of the attack, the first important decision is whether
44	you stay put or get away." Here, the citizens are empowered and expected to be proactive
45	and "[u]se common sense and available information" to prepare and evacuate. Later in
46	the paragraph, it is explicitly stated that the authorities will not be able to immediately
47	guide citizens in evacuation. Hence where there is a lack of government involvement, an
48	increased citizen involvement is encouraged to make up the loss and in Singapore's case
49	we see the opposite scenario where an increased government role almost diminishes the
50	involvement of citizens.
51	 When one does evacuate, both websites expect certain items to be prepared in
52	advance by citizens. Ready America has dedicated an entire `Get a kit' section to these
53	items. This greatly emphasises the kit's importance and goes to suggest that survival may
54	well depend on these items. On the top of the page we see "When preparing for a possible
55	emergency situation, it's best to think first about the basics of survival..." The rather
56	symbolically advising words and tone in this suggestive phrase encourages proactiveness
57	and high level of citizen preparation, increases importance of preparing the items on the
58	list. The list of items itself is expansive and comprises of many items, in particular we
59	can see some basics such as food and water are expected to be stockpiled for up to three
60	days worth for the entire family. This implies independence since families are expected to
61	be self sufficient for three days and a reason for this required self sufficiency is because
62	government expects it may not be able to provide for sufficiently in this aspect and hence
63	this can be interpreted as a suggestive forewarning for higher preparation on the citizen's
64	 Page 2 of 6
65	part. Ready Singapore, on the other hand, adopts a different approach to this preparation
66	of essential items. The site places the mainly concentrates on the concept of a `Ready
67	Bag'. This bag is required to contain only essential items such as identification
68	documents, a medical card and essentials such as torchlight and a radio. This bag is more
69	designed for compactness and portability hence the absolute minimal amount of items has
70	been included. In comparison to America's `Emergency Kit' this seems rather meagre
71	and on its own it may not be much use. However if complemented with high government
72	involvement, these items would be most useful to government authorities to identify and
73	direct the people where necessary, so this type of minimal preparation implies active
74	government involvement to bridge the gap by providing the required necessities. Under
75	the civil defence section of the website there are links to pages from the SCDF website
76	which clearly lay out procedures for food, fuel and water rationing. The words chosen on
77	the link itself `Where to go, what to do' is authoritative and suggests a rather step by step
78	`spoon feed' approach which requires little or no preparation on the citizen's part. This is
79	a concrete example of high government involvement that reduces the need for excessive
80	preparation by citizens since in times of need these schemes will come in to bridge the
81	gap.
82	 No doubt Ready Singapore also, has a similar list found inside the SCDF
83	handbook as comprehensive to Ready America's kit. However the emphasis placed on
84	the Ready Bag was much greater, since the more comprehensive list was not actually
85	directly linked. The fact that the website undermines the importance of the
86	comprehensive list by the lack of pronounced attention and access possibly implies that
87	the government perceives such preparation items may not be of significant importance, in
88	fact excessive stockpiling even may cause prevailing government efforts unable provide
89	items effectively to citizens. Hence we see due to the presence of government schemes
90	and involvement and citizen preparation needed is reduced.
91	 The management and role of children in an emergency is another area that is
92	affected by government participation. In America Kids, we see a colourful and attractive
93	sub-site that is dedicated to children and easy for them to identify with. In this site the
94	emphasis is placed on children and we are presented with tailor-made games to inculcate
95	the preparation skills and emergency drills involved. For example the simple `Pack it up'
96	 Page 3 of 6
97	game goes a long way in helping children identify essential items and greatly involving
98	them in the preparation process. Another example would be the catch phrase `Graduate
99	from Readiness U', which symbolically increases importance of preparation by allowing
100	children to relate this preparation to their schooling life and the all importance of
101	graduation which is appreciated and viewed by children as an important goal in their
102	lives, further allows children to draw connections and realise importance of preparation.
103	This suggests that the government believes even the involvement of children promotes
104	cohesiveness and the preparation needed to help families be self sufficient and survive
105	emergencies. The need for this self sufficiency again signifies lack adequate of
106	government involvement to be able to effectively reach the masses hence the reiteration
107	and stress on higher levels of preparation by, in this case, children. In comparison
108	children's section of Ready Singapore - the Kiddy Bag is much less alluring to children
109	and more aimed at the children's parents. Within this area of the site we see fewer
110	pictures and perhaps more words than the America's Ready Kids sections. Here we see
111	less emphasis on the actual preparation done by the children (implied by obvious lack of
112	material directed towards children) and instead some preparation required by the parents
113	to help authorities to effectively manage children. This is shown clearly when we find
114	that the Kiddy bag actually contains items that would be more useful to the rescue
115	workers: for example, the easily identifiable cap and whistle will draw their attention
116	while the teddy bear or soft toy will help the workers pacify the child. So the government
117	involvement again is shown to be active with the minimal response by citizens, which is
118	designed to aid authorities and in fact almost no necessary or stipulated response by
119	children, which again is the opposite of America's scenario where children are expected
120	to contribute actively to relieve some of the burden from the parents.
121	 Both websites also contain comprehensive information about the actual threats
122	themselves and systematically categorise the various possible threats their respective
123	countries might face. No doubt most of Ready Singapore's threat information is linked to
124	the Learn Civil Defence page, something arguably outside the website, the information is
125	still easily accessible from Ready Singapore via hyperlinks and the lack of any such
126	information on the Ready Singapore page itself implies that readers instinctively refer to
127	the site in their quest for more information. In the case of Ready.gov the `Be informed'
128	 Page 4 of 6
129	section plays a similar role. On the page we see a very simple picture of a woman alone
130	on the top. The important issue here is that the woman is shown alone, no one else just
131	the woman alone looking straight at the reader. This unintentionally symbolises solitude
132	and perhaps suggests that the reader may face the emergency alone just like this woman.
133	This could subtly bring a sense of urgency and further promote a higher level of
134	preparation when the reader identifies with the huge amount of preparation expected. In
135	comparison to Learn Civil Defence page we see cartoon wear a scene of a model family
136	is depicted, each member of the family with their `Ready bags' and parents comforting
137	and guiding the children along. However, the key difference here is that we can see two
138	people outside the family circle: the civil defence officer and the rescue worker, which in
139	this case symbolises government participation. Unlike the America's picture of the sole
140	woman, the reader would be more likely to be comforted and acknowledges the presence
141	of government agents. This subtly depicts the reduced participation of citizens (unlike in
142	America's case) since the presence of the Civil Defence and rescue workers seem more
143	dominating and in an emergency situation no doubt they will be more commanding as
144	well.
145	 In conclusion government involvement does have a significant effect on the level
146	of participation of citizens in the response towards a threat as demonstrated by the two
147	websites. With a higher level of government involvement the citizen participation will be
148	diminished and vice versa. No doubt it may not be the only factor affecting the citizen
149	participation but nonetheless it is a major one with, by far the most influence.
150	Works Cited
151	Ready America - http://www.ready.gov/
152	Ready Singapore - http://www2.mha.gov.sg/mha/getready/index.html

162	Loss of the White Knight and the Chosen One in the game of morality.
163	The reversing of roles in Star Wars Episode 3: Revenge of the Sith and The Dark Knight
164	Movies that usually have a plot portraying a struggle between good and evil will have a distinction
165	between the two forces where one group of characters will represent "good" while the other will represent
166	"evil". The distinction between the two groups is generally tied to their beliefs and behaviorism which in
167	the case of "good", characters belonging to this group will tend to believe in values such as justice and
168	peace. In addition, they are seen to be protecting the society presented in the imagined world of the movie
169	from potential threats. On the other hand, "evil" characters are usually seen to be disrupting the peace that
170	the good characters are trying to uphold by creating chaos and suffering to all members in the imagined
171	world of the movie.
172	The above can be seen in both George Lucas's Star Wars Episode 3: Revenge of the Sith and Christopher
173	Nolan's The Dark Knight. In Lucas's movie, the character Anakin Skywalker, a Jedi Knight is part of a
174	group of sentient beings called the Jedi in which members aim to uphold peace in the galaxy through
175	 1
176	vigilance and protectorship. The Jedi are seen to be representing the forces of good whereas Chancellor
177	Palaptine who is a Sith Lord in disguise, is a polar opposite of the Jedi and a schemer who is threatening
178	the interests of the Jedi and therefore represents "evil". In Nolan's movie, the character Harvey Dent, a
179	district attorney works together with the main protagonist, Batman and the Gotham City's police force led
180	by Lieutenant James Gordon and together they represent the forces of "good" who maintain the security
181	of Gotham City's citizens. They are in conflict with the Joker, a psychotic villain who brings about chaos
182	and fear into the heart of Gotham City and thus represents "evil". However, one would question the
183	simple distinction between good and evil. By comparing the two characters, Anakin and Harvey, one
184	would notice their eventual fall from grace and mutilation by fire into the antagonists, Darth Vader and
185	Two-Face respectively. There is no doubt that manipulation by evil is key in corrupting both characters
186	and causing them to stray away from good. But is manipulation as potent and encompassing such that
187	individual morality is decimated entirely? Besides a pull towards evil, are there other forces that could
188	have pushed them away from good? In this essay, I will argue that although manipulation is effective in
189	corrupting both Anakin and Harvey, there is another force that pushes both characters from good which is
190	the inability of the forces of good to resolve the inner struggles that both characters face. In addition, both
191	characters have a weak sense of morality that makes them susceptible to these push and pull forces. A
192	weak sense of morality causes both characters to be unable to resist the pull of manipulation and together
193	with the push from the forces of good, results in their eventual conversion to evil.
194	The role of manipulator is central in both movies where evil lures both Anakin and Harvey into
195	temptations that will ultimately destroy their identity as "good". In Lucas's movie, Palpatine plays on
196	Anakin's insecurities and deceives him into believing that only Palpatine has the solution to his fears.
197	Palpatine constantly plays on Anakin's fear of Padme's death. Palpatine hints that he knows "what has
198	been troubling you" and offers him a solution. "Learn to know the dark side of the Force, Anakin, and
199	you will be able to save your wife from certain death." In order to achieve the power of the dark side, one
200	 2
201	has to commit merciless acts of slaughter which transgresses the values and beliefs of the Jedi. Palpatine
202	convinces Anakin that he has to "wipe out" all who stand in the way of the Sith which includes the Jedi
203	and only then will Anakin be empowered by the dark side which will enable him to "save" Padme. Hence,
204	Anakin chooses to believe in Palpatine, adopts the new role, Darth Vader and proceeds onto the path of
205	slaughter. On the other hand, in Nolan's film, the Joker drives Harvey to madness by mocking his
206	righteous status and using Rachel's death to unleash Harvey's vengeance. In the hospital scene where
207	Harvey is recuperating from his injuries, the Joker appears and taunts him that no matter how heroic
208	Harvey and the forces of good are, they are still not able to save Rachel. Furthermore, the Joker explains
209	that he is not the cause of Rachel's death. The Joker refers to himself as "a dog chasing cars. I wouldn't
210	know what to do with one if I caught it." He subtly hints that it is the traitors in Harvey's own forces that
211	are responsible for assisting in the kidnap of both Rachel and Harvey and are the cause of Rachel's death
212	and his disfigurement. The traitors are two police detectives, Words and Ramirez who are also working
213	for a crime lord, Salvatore Maroni who is in cahoots with the Joker. Harvey, adopting his alter ego, Two-
214	Face, goes into a mindless rage and attempts to exert his revenge on all who were responsible for
215	Rachel's death through an irrational manner - Flipping a coin to determine the victim's fate. Hence he
216	fulfills the Joker's intentions of driving "Gotham's white knight" to madness. Therefore, both characters
217	are seen to be manipulated and corrupted by evil and set onto a path of no return.
218	However manipulation on its own is not sufficient to pull both characters over to evil. An important force
219	that pushes them away from good is the fact the forces of good are unable to provide a solution or reason
220	that both characters can accept in response to their respective inner struggles. This can be seen in the case
221	of both characters where they have a lover who they cannot bear to lose through death. The fear of loss of
222	their lovers is compounded by the fact that the lovers hold an important place in the characters' lives. This
223	is due to a strong emotional attachment forged between the two characters and their lovers where Padme
224	Amidala, is seen to be Anakin's wife whereas Rachel Dawes, is seen to be a love interest that Harvey is
225	 3
226	pursuing. In Anakin's case, he had a dream where he envisioned Padme dying in labor and is disturbed by
227	the premonition. The premonition reminds Anakin of another past premonition that foretold the death of
228	his mother and he fears that the current premonition would materialize just like how it did for his mother.
229	Out of concern, Anakin seeks the advice of a Jedi Master named Yoda. Instead of providing a solution to
230	save Padme from death, Yoda simply advices Anakin that "death is a natural part of life" and Anakin has
231	to "learn to let go". Yoda's advice contrasts starkly with Palpatine's promise in which Palpatine claims
232	that he can in fact save Padme but only if Anakin chooses to ally himself with him. The fact that it is not
233	Yoda but Palpatine who is able to provide the ideal solution that Anakin is seeking for only serves to push
234	Anakin away from the Jedi and to succumb to evil. On the other hand, in Harvey's case, the Joker
235	succeeds in killing Rachel as both Batman and Gordan fail in rescuing her. Harvey is devastated and
236	blames Gordon for failing to listen to him when he tried to warn him earlier regarding the traitors in their
237	offices that he believes could have prevented Rachel's death. When Gordon tries to reason with Harvey
238	that he could not save Rachel despite trying his best, Harvey violently rejects his explanation as he
239	strongly feels that Gordon could have saved Rachel if "he stood up against corruption" which suggests
240	that Harvey wants Gordon to be held responsible. Furthermore, when Harvey laments on the unfairness
241	of his plight, he questions both Batman and Gordon, "why is it me who is the only one that lost
242	everything?" When Batman tries to reason with Harvey that it is in fact the Joker's plans to cause
243	Harvey's downfall, Harvey is seen to not accept the truth but in fact resorts to madness by shooting
244	Batman and threatening to kill Gordon's son next. Harvey rejects the rationale of good but chooses to
245	believe in evil and the words of the Joker who suggests that chaos is the only thing that is fair. Harvey
246	considers the reasons and justifications of both Batman and Gordon to be both unfair and unacceptable.
247	This resentment only pushes him further away from good and into the ways of evil that he ironically
248	considers to be fair and just.
249	 4
250	Although both push and pull forces can be seen in the eventual shift to evil for both characters, a weak
251	sense of morality in both characters is necessary to facilitate this shift. This is because if both characters
252	have a strong sense of morality, it will not be easy for them to be swayed over to evil. If the characters
253	have a strong sense of morality that enables them to consistently differentiate right from wrong, they will
254	be able to resist the temptations of the manipulator and at the same time be able to rationalize the reasons
255	put forth by the forces of good. Unfortunately this is not the case in both characters. For Anakin, he is
256	seen to be indecisive in his actions which translate to an inconsistency in his morality. Anakin seems to be
257	aware of the consequences of his actions but is easily persuaded into committing the wrong action. For
258	example in the scene where Anakin is contemplating whether to slay a Sith Lord named Count Dooku, he
259	is seen to be hesitating as he knows that "it's not the Jedi way" to kill an "unarmed prisoner". Yet when
260	Palpatine simply commands him to "do it", Anakin follows blindly without question. This clearly shows
261	that Anakin does not have a strong will to resist the corruption of evil and is easily manipulated by
262	Palpatine. On the other hand for Harvey, he has a warped sense of morality where he is seen to be
263	obsessed with the notion of flipping a coin to determine his choice of actions. The simple flip of a coin
264	suggests that he does not put much thought into his actions and morality does not govern them but rather
265	"chance". For example, when the Joker uses Harvey' obsession with chance against him, Harvey swiftly
266	adopts the role of Two-Face believing that justice has failed and concludes, "the world is cruel, and the
267	only morality in a cruel world is chance. Unbiased. Unprejudiced. Fair." Harvey takes his own obsession
268	to the extreme, disregarding the basis of morality and flips a coin to determine the fate of his victims.
269	When the coin lands on the charred face, Two-Face simply murders his victims in cold blood without
270	second thought. The fact that Harvey leaves a human's life to chance serves to highlight his decadent state
271	and the embrace of the villainous Two-Face role.
272	In sum, a weak sense of morality opens both Anakin and Harvey to a combination of both push and pull
273	forces that are paramount in shifting their allegiance from good to evil. The role of the manipulator can be
274	 5
275	explained through a simple analogy such as a game of Reversi where the manipulator is seen to be
276	"reversing" as many game pieces to his side which is a parallel to the way he corrupts the forces of good.
277	However this is not to say that the manipulator is the only force that is pulling these two characters
278	towards him but rather the fact that forces of good are accountable for pushing their own forces away and
279	into the path of evil. Just like in a game of Reversi, it requires two players and one player will capitalize
280	on the other player's mistake. A grave mistake could cost him the entire game and in the case of both
281	movies, the loss of both Anakin and Harvey to the forces of evil.
282	Bibliography:

284	States: 20th Century Fox, 2005.
285	Nolan, Christopher. The Dark Knight (Two-Disc Special Edition). [DVD] United States: Warner Bros.
286	Pictures, 2008.

317	The Deathly Hallows and The Prince.
318	 Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows is the final installment in J.K. Rowling's Harry
319	Potter book series. The series describes the existence of a "wizarding world" living
320	among non-magic users known as "Muggles1". In this final book, the story continues
321	with a fight that has broken out, between the Light and the Dark, within the "wizarding
322	world". Lord Voldemort with his army of Death Eaters bent on their quest of
323	conquering the wizarding world and the subjugation of the "Muggles" represent the
324	Dark side; Albus Dumbledore, Headmaster of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and
325	Wizardry, and his Order of the Phoenix resisting the advances of Voldemort represent
326	the Light. At the end of the book, the Light eventually triumphs over the Dark by
327	following through with Dumbledore's plan - one that is filled with trials and tribulations.
328	The struggle to defeat Voldemort shows the greatness of the Headmaster, but it also
329	exposes an unknown side of him. In his pursuit to vanquish his enemy, Dumbledore
330	used others without reservations. This was especially so for Severus Snape and Harry
331	Potter. Snape is the potion teacher in Hogwarts who is also Dumbledore's double agent
332	in Voldemort's camp; and Harry is the orphan of Lily and James Potter, members of
333	Dumbledore's Order of the Phoenix, and also the only survivor of Voldemort's death
334	curse.
335	 Dumbledore fully aware that his plan to thwart Voldemort would lead to the
336	death of Snape and Harry had no compunction in tricking them into believing him. He
337	made them trust him blindly and to do his bidding just so that they can fulfill his purpose
338	and then "die at the right moment2" that he had planned for them. While many may

2	 folio 7 (2008): 16-21
3	 Explaining the Instability of Power
4	 in The Truman Show
5	 Ng Si Ying Pamela
6	 ___________________________________________________________________________
7	 In Andrew Niccol's screenplay for The Truman Show (1998), which went on to became a
8	 Paramount Pictures production directed by Peter Weir, the titular character Truman Burbank is
9	 an unknowing celebrity, the star of a television programme which has been ongoing since his
10	birth. Truman lives on an islanded set known as Seahaven, surrounded by contract actors who
11	play characters ranging from his family members to the people he passes on the street. The show
12	is broadcast live twenty-four hours a day, making Truman one of the most-watched television
13	characters in the world--people are completely taken with the addictive programme, which
14	presents a voyeuristic, no-holds-barred perspective on Truman's everyday life in all its mundane
15	details. At the start of the narrative, Truman is completely oblivious to the constructed nature of
16	the world he knows. Niccol's work traces Truman's gradual understanding of his circumstances
17	and his attempts to unravel the fiction. Many conflicts of interest may be observed--Truman
18	desires to be free and to know the truth, Christof strives to maintain command of the show,
19	while the audience is ever-ready to satisfy their thirst for entertainment. I find it most striking
20	that in negotiating these conflicts of interests, each of the three parties shifts constantly between
21	positions of empowerment and relative impotency. How is it that the seemingly clear-cut
22	placement of Christof, Truman and the viewers in their respective roles fails to create concrete
23	demarcations between those in control and those being controlled? In this essay, I will explain
24	the often simultaneous disempowerment and empowerment of the three mentioned parties in
25	order to present my thesis that absolute power for any one player in the media-driven world of
26	The Truman Show is impossible. This, in turn, is because the rise of the reality-television genre in
27	the contemporary media context creates an environment in which the power of one player is
28	always undercut by his dependence on others--hence power becomes unstable.
29	 As the mega-star of a wildly-popular television programme, Truman has great power and
30	influence over his audience and perhaps even over the commercial decisions of the television
31	network that owns the show. A useful analysis of celebrity clout comes from the work of
32	Zygmunt Bauman in Globalisation: The Human Consequences (1998). Bauman discusses the
33	empowerment of the celebrity figure by describing his elevation to an "infinitely superior" (54)
34	position. He likens the media-centric world to a large web in which the passive and localized
35	viewers--"locals" (53)--watch the celebrities who hold court apart from and above that all-
36	encompassing web. The celebrities, by virtue of their global placement, are described as the
37	"globals." Bauman envisions a system which empowers celebrities who are able to exert immense
38	influence, with telling parallels drawn between celebrity-worship and religions like Christianity.
39	Using Bauman's concept of celebrity power, one can see that Truman's ability to attract masses
40	of avid viewers and exert influence over them is reflective of his empowerment. The fact that
41	Truman is a peculiar type of celebrity--one who is totally unaware of his own celebrity--does
42	not prevent us from seeing him in a position of empowerment. If anything, Truman's ability to
43	project an influence beyond his own consciousness emphasizes the empowerment of the
44	celebrity figure through his sheer placement in the global. It is also possible to observe that
45	Truman's growing awareness of the truth comes largely from the (uneasy) realization that he
46	literally has the power to cause changes to everything around him, from traffic conditions--for
47	instance, "almost immediately, Truman encounters a traffic snarl" (59) when he attempts to drive
48	out of Seahaven--to the manner in which the other actors behave around him. This reflects on
49	Truman's part an understanding of his power even before he realizes fully the implications of his
50	celebrity.
51	 Even so, Truman's empowerment as discussed above is neither complete nor
52	permanent. As a celebrity figure and the star of a reality-television show, he faces the problem of
53	constant attention from both the audience and the creators of the show. Their collective gaze
54	 1
55	 folio 7 (2008): 16-21
56	clearly disconcerts him when he first becomes aware of this--he says, warily, that "everyone
57	seems to be in on it" (Niccol 67) and "the eyes are everywhere" (105). These utterances reveal his
58	uneasiness at what seems like an overwhelmingly conspiratorial attempt to invade his private
59	space. While Bauman's analysis can help explain Truman's empowerment by likening the
60	celebrity to a privileged status similar to that of "royalty" (Bauman 54), it cannot account for
61	Truman's apparent helplessness against the kind of massive intrusion of privacy which is
62	experienced as a consequence of that elevation in status. Truman is, after all, not a celebrity in the
63	way Bauman understands. The celebrity in Bauman's argument is less intruded upon because the
64	media context he writes of is not really an "interactive" (53) one; instead, it is a limited
65	"interactive one-way medium," where the viewer comes into play (interacts) only as far as the
66	celebrity chooses to allow it. All significant action in the media process thus originates from the
67	celebrity alone, and his/her elevated status above the level of the "locals" is stable. Like "royalty"
68	(54), these celebrities are likely to be seen only under the most carefully chosen and orchestrated
69	circumstances. They are thus able selectively to limit the vulnerability that exposure to the public
70	eye entails while being empowered indefinitely by their ability to influence the viewers, to whom
71	any real ability to participate actively--that is, interactively (53)--is denied. However, the
72	celebrity in Niccol's work is unable to control the degree to which that interactivity exists across
73	the proverbial television screen because of the constancy with which the viewer gets to observe
74	the celebrity (Truman). Non-stop surveillance in a twenty-four hour live programme presents
75	here the reality-television genre in its gross extreme. Although Truman appears empowered
76	according to Bauman's conception of celebrity clout, he is also notably disempowered by the fact
77	that he cannot control when or how he is seen by the audience. This is where the celebrity power
78	that Bauman envisions ends, where a new kind of celebrity power which is constantly and
79	perhaps equally contested by disempowerment through the loss of privacy begins for the reality-
80	television celebrity.
81	 Considering where Niccol's screenplay departs from Bauman's concise distinction
82	between the celebrity and his audience also reveals the ambiguous position of the viewers in
83	Niccol's work. In the light of their obvious fascination with "The Truman Show," the viewers of
84	celebrity come across as feeble players in the media game, unable to act except in accordance
85	with their addiction to the programme. The screenplay is interspersed with brief but telling
86	scenes of Truman's audience enthralled by whatever Truman happens to be doing. In "a bar
87	somewhere" (Niccol 56) patrons discuss the show enthusiastically while "two old ladies" (63) in
88	"a living room somewhere" share a moment of tension as they observe Truman trying to leave
89	the set in his automobile--their actions and emotions are dictated by what happens in Truman's
90	life. The viewers of "The Truman Show" in Niccol's work seem, then, to fill the ranks of the
91	"locals" (Bauman 53) who are hooked to the network from their own homes across the country.
92	Their watching appears to be an act of immobilization--they are transfixed and metaphorically
93	imprisoned (54) by their adoration of "globals" (53) like Truman (the celebrity). Yet there are
94	also many instances in Niccol's work where members of the audience actively assert themselves.
95	Sylvia, a former cast member who comes close to "telling [Truman] the truth" (Niccol 36) about
96	his world, confronts the makers of "The Truman Show" with "thinly disguised resentment" (80)
97	because she disagrees with what she perceives as the imprisonment of Truman in his constructed
98	world. Others attempt to infiltrate the set so as to be on television, to cross the division between
99	celebrity and ordinariness--these include a man "bursting from a large Christmas parcel" and a
100	parachutist with the message "Truman, you're on TV" on his chest (73). These may be
101	understood as actual, physical attempts on the part of the audience to rise above the passivity
102	noted by Bauman in explicating the resigned paralysis of the "watchers" (Bauman 52)--"pure
103	and unalloyed watching is their lot" (53).
104	 In Niccol's work, such a state of powerlessness is not what awaits the watcher of
105	celebrity. The Truman Show introduces the idea of a consumer palate which has become numbed
106	by the sheer variety of entertainment materials made available to them, and which must then be
107	tempted by new materials--reality-television--designed to suit their tastes. It also reveals the rise
108	of a desire on the part of the viewer to gain entrance into the world of the celebrity, to gain that
109	proverbial one minute of fame. Note how Bauman actually depicts the willingness of the
110	audience to become part of a viewer-ship as the consequence of an insidious persuasion--the
111	media "seduces people into watching" (52). Since the audience must be seduced, coaxed rather
112	 2
113	 folio 7 (2008): 16-21
114	than violently "forced" into their positions of powerlessness, the basis upon which they
115	surrender their power actually reflects the power of consumerism which, while less crucial in
116	Bauman's analysis, is instrumental in understanding the ability of the audience in The Truman Show
117	to take a strong stand despite their apparent distance from the action. In Niccol's screenplay, the
118	basis upon which the viewer is seduced has changed--this is but part of a larger consumer
119	revolution in the contemporary media context. From being inert admirers of lofty celebrity ideals,
120	the audience member now wants to watch himself or herself (or someone just like them) on the
121	television screen. It is no coincidence, then, that Christof refers to "The Truman Show" as "a
122	mirror" (Niccol 75) when speculating on the reasons behind the show's immense popularity.
123	Indeed, Christof tells Truman, "you were real. That's what made you so good to watch." The
124	audiences of the reality-television programme are attracted to Truman not because he seems
125	exceptional but because he reflects a life which is familiar and identifiable. A reality-television
126	programme such as "The Truman Show" allows the watchers to take a more active role in the
127	process of watching because it allows for and showcases the possibility of transgressing the
128	boundaries that keep the watchers local and the celebrities global. In other words, the audience
129	desires a form of entertainment in which the celebrity could now be an ordinary person. Reality-
130	television thus delivers in response to current consumer preferences.
131	 Finally, standing between the viewers and Truman is the middleman-of-sorts, Christof.
132	Referring to Bauman's analysis of a media-centric world, one may understand Christof as the
133	"supplier" (53), the provider of a framework within which the viewers may plug into the world of
134	the celebrity: Truman. Bauman does not clearly stipulate the degree to which this supplier is
135	empowered, perhaps conflating this role with that of the celebrity who also supplies choices to
136	the audience. In any case, Bauman clearly places the supplier in a position of empowerment, and
137	it is not difficult to see why. Christof is ostensibly in full control of the constructed world of
138	Truman in Seahaven as a godlike figure, as implied by his name which contains the word
139	"Christ." This is an impression which is only enhanced by the admiration of many adoring fans
140	who revere Christof for giving them Truman--callers on a talk-show say "it's a great honor"
141	(Niccol 76) to speak to Christof. We must, however, also recognize the less-than-almighty
142	aspects of Christof in Niccol's work. What he does, essentially, is to respond to the watchers'
143	desires in a commercial or (as he prefers to think) artistic way, although he does take an
144	extraordinary personal and paternal interest in Truman, who is the physical embodiment of a
145	brainchild which has become a runaway success. Christof is himself keenly aware of the
146	importance of the audience, having created avenues for "product placement" (Niccol 78) in "The
147	Truman Show," and also negotiating issues of "ratings" (74) and sustaining a "core audience"
148	(54). Additionally, it is apparent that Christof is overpowered by Truman by virtue of Truman's
149	vast commercial value and also, perhaps to a lesser extent, because of his paternal sentiments
150	towards Truman. The screenplay makes it clear in several scenes that Truman exercises great, if
151	indirect, power over Christof, who is forced to shape both the environment and the plot
152	according to Truman's behavior. As Truman attempts to leave Seahaven in frustration, obvious
153	obstacles are caused to spring up in response to Truman's actions, and these include "a 20 foot
154	high wall of flame" which "shoots" up "as if someone flicked on a gas switch" (Niccol 61)--a
155	description which confirms both the enormity of Truman's actions in the eyes of Christof and
156	the exaggerated efficiency with which Christof will respond to Truman's whims. This is further
157	evidenced in Christof's constantly having to rework the script to neutralize Truman's suspicions,
158	even to the extent of reviving a dead character for Truman's sake against his own better
159	judgment, reinstating Kirk, Truman's fictional father, even though it would be "the first time that
160	an intruder has been rewarded with a starring role" (73). Christof is thus by no means a possessor
161	of absolute, god-like power. If he is a god, he is only a minor one, ever-conscious of the
162	fickleness of his followers and also of the fact that he is loved only as far as the father is loved as
163	the creator of the son: Truman and "The Truman Show."
164	 Niccol's screenplay thus presents power in a media-centric, contemporary context as
165	being shared in varying proportions amongst its players, with no easy dichotomies between the
166	powerful and the powerless. This sort of unstable power seems to resist the constraints of
167	theoretical postulations about empowerment and disempowerment. In considering the
168	application of Bauman's analysis in the context of Niccol's screenplay, it quickly becomes
169	apparent that Bauman's conception of celebrity explains some, but not all aspects of the
170	 3
171	 folio 7 (2008): 16-21
172	empowerment and emasculation of the various players in the media game. This forces us to
173	recognize that the media context of The Truman Show is one which differs greatly from that of
174	Bauman's understanding, and to acknowledge the rise of the reality-television genre as a complex
175	and groundbreaking expression of unstable power in the hands of the celebrity (Truman), the
176	media mogul (Christof) and the audience. Such fluidity and flexibility in the acquiring and
177	management of power may well be the hallmark of the media industry today, where rapid
178	changes in function and the interdependence of various actors characterize all manners of
179	activities.
180	Works cited
181	Bauman, Zygmunt. Globalization: The Human Consequences. New York: Columbia University Press,
182	 1998.
183	Niccol, Andrew. The Truman Show: the Shooting Script. London: Nick Hern, 1998.
