188	 A Flicker of Rebellion
189	 Tham Shu Ting
190	 ___________________________________________________________________________
191	 George Orwell's 1984 is a terrifying depiction of a dystopian world shrouded in gloom, decay
192	 and fear. The story is set in Oceania, one of the three existing countries constantly at war with
193	Geach other. This totalitarian society is ruled by an elusive figure called Big Brother who leads
194	the section of the Party comprising his closest followers, the inner Party, and the rest of the
195	"comrades" who form the outer Party. In total, the Party makes up fifteen percent of the
196	population of Oceania, with the remaining citizens, who are known as the Proles, practically
197	disregarded and condemned to the "gutters" (Orwell 71). "No attempt [is] made to indoctrinate
198	them with the ideology of the Party" (71) because they are deemed "beneath suspicion" (72). All
199	Party members, on the other hand, hold strong to the idea that Big Brother is their sole provider
200	of support, their comfort, and even their reason for being alive. They live a strictly regimented
201	existence with everything dictated from above, from attire to food to the activities they take part
202	in. They practically live in fear of not conforming to what is deemed the Party norm because any
203	sign of unorthodoxy is perceived as "thoughtcrime": the crime of not complying with the
204	restrictions imposed on all Party members.
205	 Considering the presence of such an overwhelming and omnipresent dictatorial force, it
206	then seems striking that there is so little rebellion against it. What actually keeps these citizens of
207	Oceania rooted to the veneration of Big Brother and his dominance? Are they not disillusioned
208	and discontented with the pall of darkness and total domination engulfing them, with having to
209	lead restricted lives which deprive them of even simple pleasures and desires such that their sole
210	concern becomes the well-being of Big Brother? It is the overwhelming nature of the methods of
211	power wielded by the Party over the individual, which makes use of all levels of control, cutting
212	across the social, economic, political and cultural spheres, that causes Party members to feel that
213	they will never be able to outdo the Party, and this fear is enough to deter most from rebellion.
214	The fact that the Party has such harsh control over every single aspect of life enables us to use
215	French sociologist Michel Foucault's exposition of a similar method of control--panoptical
216	power--as a theoretical construct with which to understand the methods of control Big Brother
217	has over the Party.
218	 The Panopticon is an architectural model of a prison conceptualised by eighteenth-
219	century philosopher Jeremy Bentham as a system of "an `all-seeing' power" (Foucault 152). In
220	the overall scheme, "each comrade becomes an overseer" (152), where all prisoners watch one
221	another. Such continual checks on one another result in "total and circulating mistrust" (158),
222	and so heighten the need for individuals to conform to acceptable behaviour in order to avoid
223	punishment. This concept of a panoptic gaze is examined closely by Foucault, as documented in
224	the interview "The Eye of Power." There are a number of similarities in the motives and
225	implementation of power in the case of both Oceania and the system of the Panopticon. For
226	example, power in both is emphasised by "gaining access to individuals themselves, to their
227	bodies, their gestures and all their daily actions" (Foucault 152). In addition, control, "even when
228	faced with ruling a multiplicity of men, could be as efficacious as if it were being exercised over a
229	single one." Foucault's interpretation of the panoptical power attached to extremely stringent
230	control over every single thought and behaviour enables us to understand how Big Brother
231	controls the entire Party. This explains why revolt against such coerced conformity is practically
232	non-existent.
233	 The most noticeable form of control exerted is the overwhelming use of surveillance.
234	"Every sound you made was overheard, and, except in darkness, every moment scrutinized"
235	(Orwell 3). This is made possible with the many telescreens--monitors tracked by the Thought
236	Police which receive and transmit simultaneously--put in place at almost every conceivable
237	angle. Such a system is highly effective in preventing rebellion because its purpose is "not so
238	much to punish wrongdoers as to prevent even the possibility of wrongdoing, by immersing
239	 1
240	 folio 7 (2008): 42-46
241	people in a field of total visibility where the opinion, observation and discourse of others would
242	restrain them from harmful acts" (Foucault 153). This incredible transparency nips unorthodoxy
243	in the bud, with the intention of preventing rather than later dealing with misconduct, thus
244	allowing the authorities a tighter grip over their people. As an example, Winston, the protagonist
245	in the novel who is fighting hard to rebel against the Party, is well aware of the perceptiveness of
246	the gaze cast upon him and is constantly adjusting "his features into the expression of quiet
247	optimism which was advisable to wear when facing the telescreen" (Orwell 5) because even "a
248	single flicker of the eyes could give you away" (37).
249	 It is impossible for rebels not to get caught due to the total transparency of their actions
250	and expressions; thus the authorities share Bentham's formula of "power through transparency"
251	and "subjection by `illumination'" (Foucault 154). There is an ever-present, ever-watching and
252	intruding gaze. So even though Winston might have initially evaded the watchful eye of the
253	Thought Police, his continuous attempts at insurgency and increased complacency at being
254	successful at each round eventually result in his capture. With such effective control over those
255	who would resist, it is common knowledge among Party members that one is considered dead
256	the minute one commits even a thoughtcrime. For offenders against the Party, the penalty of
257	being vaporised is definite, and it is only a question of when one will be annihilated. As a result,
258	this absolute action is enough to scare most into feeble submission, and immediately lashing out
259	at the consciousness of those even vaguely expressing disinterest in the Party.
260	 Therefore the Party's method of surveillance against rebellion is further enhanced by
261	another level of security. The Party has ingeniously created a self-circulating system of checks
262	among the comrades. This is "an inspecting gaze, a gaze which each individual under its weight
263	will end by interiorising to the point that he is his own overseer, each individual thus exercising
264	this surveillance over, and against, himself" (Foucault 155). This additional supervision, which we
265	may, following Foucault, term interiorisation, is a self-reproach mechanism, where the suspecting
266	gaze is so powerful that it causes those who are being watched to become conscious of
267	themselves. Members have to act according to Party norms and since it is expected of each Party
268	comrade to be loyal to Big Brother, everyone is willing and even eager to denounce a suspected
269	insurgent immediately to the Thought Police without batting an eyelid, and betraying any remote
270	sense of friendship. The crafty authorities have installed this social "apparatus of total and
271	circulating mistrust" (158), which by its nature consists of everyone's participation regardless of
272	whether it is voluntary or otherwise. As a result, Party members learn not to trust anyone and the
273	threat of an unsuspected watchful eye cultivates a self-checking (interiorising) mechanism in
274	individuals.
275	 Even family units, traditionally bound by deep kinship and trust, do not escape the evils
276	of this system. The children, who " adored the Party and everything connected with it" (Orwell
277	24) because it "was all a sort of glorious game to them," are trained as Spies of the Thought
278	Police. Eager to please and devoid of any reservations or sense of guilt which come with
279	maturity, the young "ungovernable little savages" watch their parents "night and day for
280	symptoms of unorthodoxy." The unyielding zest of these young Spies even makes it "almost
281	normal for people over thirty to be frightened of their own children." Consequently, members
282	exist alone, as individuals, but are essentially united in a common goal, serving under the big
283	umbrella of the Party.
284	 Rebellion against such a totalitarian system and organisation is well-nigh impossible,
285	more so when individuals exist alone. That is why even Winston, who is so steadfast in his
286	resolve to resist the Party that he would have "gladly" (Orwell 125) contracted leprosy or syphilis,
287	or do "anything to rot, to weaken, to undermine" the Party, is desperate to find fellow-rebels first
288	before embarking on a revolt because he knows that individual attempts will only be in vain.
289	However, the Party's "enemies, if it had any enemies, had no way of coming together or even of
290	identifying one another" (69). This is because the authorities are astute enough to pit everyone
291	against each other, eliminating collaboration of any kind and instead encouraging a culture of
292	total suspicion among Party members. This leaves them in a bitter state of absolute mistrust of
293	one another. Ironically, it leads to nothing but total loyalty towards the Party instead. That is why,
294	as Winston rightly claims, "you did not have friends nowadays, you had comrades" (48)--a
295	relation formed out of loyalty to the Party.
296	 2
297	 folio 7 (2008): 42-46
298	 Detractors may say that there are too many crucial differences between Foucault's "The
299	Eye of Power" and Orwell's 1984 for us to be able to compare the two and to use the former as
300	a lens for reading the latter. In Oceania, the "system of power takes a pyramidical form" where
301	"there is an apex" (Foucault 159) at which Big Brother stands. There exists a form of
302	monarchical power whereby "all power derives as though from a luminous focus." On the other
303	hand, the Panoptical system revolves around a loose scheme of equality in which "no reliance
304	can be placed on a single individual" (158) and in, contrast to the Party, there is "no absolute
305	point" at the top from which control is issued. The amount of power that is wielded varies
306	between the different levels of people within the structure, but power is evenly distributed
307	between individuals on the same level. For example the prison guards stand on par with each
308	other when it comes to the level of authority they have over the prisoners. The inmates on the
309	other hand have an equal amount of power, but only over each other.
310	 Although there is a contrast in the organisation of power, there still is an important basis
311	for comparison because the ability of the authorities to induce fear is the key instrument of
312	power in both cases. Fear is internalised through the process of interiorisation--the existence of
313	an innate fear of rebuke. The prisoners in the Panopticon have no choice but to watch and
314	restrict themselves in order to avoid punishment in a very transparent environment. Moreover, in
315	Oceania Party members conform to the required social norm and constantly check to see if they
316	appear out of place for fear of triggering the suspicions of the Thought Police. In addition to
317	involuntary interiorisation, the Party also uses a display of "spectacular" (Foucault 155) violence
318	and punishment, which can come in the form of public hangings, shame and condemnation of
319	those who do not sufficiently exercise the inward-checking mechanism. Thus "The Eye of
320	Power" is applicable to 1984 and comparisons are still justified because the central focus of
321	generating fear to maintain control is consistent in both cases. Ultimately, as control creeps up in
322	all spaces and forms imaginable, it diminishes the opportunity and extinguishes the fire of an
323	individual to resist, condemning rebellion to an obscure minority. What is left is a "hollow"
324	(Orwell 256) shell devoid of thought and purpose except to serve the common good of the Party.
325	Works Cited
326	Orwell, George. 1984. New York: Signet, 1950.
327	Foucault, Michel. "The Eye of Power." Power/Knowledge. Trans. Colin Gordon et. al. New York:
328	 Pantheon, 1980.

# Sample Paper 2 Essays: Structural Breakdowns

Nine student essays from the course materials:
- **Lens:** Defending Rohan, National or Global?, Deathly Hallows and the Prince, Truman Show (Folio), A Flicker of Rebellion (Folio)
- **Comparative:** Power in Propaganda, Relationships of Power, Government Involvement in Emergencies, White Knight and the Chosen One

The Corber and Oakes PDFs are published readings, not student essays, so they're left out.

"Background / framework" means the section between the intro and R1 that either backs up the context/motive claims or sets out the theory the main reasons rely on.

---

## 1. Defending Rohan, Fangorn and the Shire (Lens)
**Texts:** *The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers* (film) + Ernest Renan, "What is a Nation?"

**Context:** Opens with the dictionary definition of "community." In the film, Elves, Hobbits, Men and Ents work together to defend their land against a shared threat. Defending the community looks *instinctive*, like self-preservation: Rohan's citizens defend their country, and Aragorn's "women and children," without questioning why.

**Motive:** This apparently *innate* urge contradicts Renan, who implies such feelings are *nurtured*. For Renan, a nation is a "moral conscience" created by people, an imagined community.

**Thesis:** Read through Renan, defending one's homeland is fundamentally different from protecting oneself. The first comes from belonging to a community; the second is inborn.
+268 more lines
I've written up all nine sample essays in [Sample_Essay_Breakdowns.md](Sample_Essay_Breakdowns.md). Each one is broken down into context, motive, thesis, background/framework, R1, R2 and so on, acknowledgement/response, conclusion, and the instructor's comments where they were included. The Corber and Oakes PDFs are published readings rather than student essays, so I left them out.

At a glance


EssayTypeMotive (the puzzle)Thesis (core)Background / frameworkMain reasonsAcknowledgement / response
Defending RohanLens: LOTR + RenanDefending the community looks innate, but Renan says it's nurturedDefending your homeland comes from belonging; protecting yourself is inbornInside the motive paragraph4: heritage, shared values, sacrifice, overlapping communitiesScope limit only
National or Global?Lens: US security strategy + Canada'sA national strategy that's about the worldIt's a global strategy led by the USNone6"Porous borders" answered with "Canada is open too"
Power in Propaganda (A-)Comparative: two WWII postersYou'd expect men over women, but power runs three ways (man, woman, narrator)The posters balance undermining and empowering men to get them to actThe context paragraph does the job3, building on each otherLimits of the posters' assumptions, in the conclusion
Relationships of PowerComparative: Duck and Cover + MooreFew apparent grounds for comparison, yet both blur teacher/adult and student/childThe relationships slip because their discourses are interconnectedOwn theory paragraph (extrinsic vs intrinsic power)5Two inside the arguments (satire/actors; why adults would play students)
Government InvolvementComparative: Ready.gov + Ready SingaporeSimilar threats, very different citizen rolesMore government involvement means less citizen involvementShort paragraph4 categories: evacuation, kits, kids, imageryInside R2 ("SCDF has a full list, but it's buried")
White KnightComparative: Star Wars III + Dark KnightIs manipulation alone enough to corrupt?Pull (manipulation) + push (good fails them) + weak moralityNone3: pull, push, preconditionR1 is the acknowledgement
Deathly HallowsLens: HP7 + The PrinceIs the leader of the Light a manipulator?Dumbledore is a Machiavellian realistLens paragraph that justifies the fit3"Feared vs loved": Dumbledore goes beyond Machiavelli
Truman Show (Folio)Lens: screenplay + BaumanEveryone swings between power and powerlessnessAbsolute power is impossible because reality TV creates dependenceBauman introduced inside R15Built into every section: where Bauman fails
A Flicker of Rebellion (Folio)Lens: 1984 + FoucaultTotal tyranny, yet hardly any rebellionControl at every level breeds a fear that deters revoltPanopticon paragraph5"Pyramid vs Panopticon" answered with "fear is central to both"

What the strongest ones have in common


  • The motive is "you'd expect X, but the text does Y." National or Global got marked down because its context never set out what's normal, so the "exception" didn't register.
  • The thesis resolves the puzzle with a "because" or a "how." National or Global's thesis was criticised for restating the motive.
  • Lens papers have a framework paragraph before R1. It introduces the theory and justifies why it fits the text.
  • The best lens papers use the lens's limits. Truman Show does this throughout, and Deathly Hallows and Flicker each give it a paragraph. Defending Rohan was told it "tried too hard" to make its lens fit.
  • The reasons build on each other rather than forming a list. Power in Propaganda and White Knight work this way; Government Involvement is a list of categories.
  • The instructor's repeated complaint is jumping from an argument's main claim straight to evidence. Add a general reason tied to each text first.

How this maps onto your top pick (vape posters + Stylianou)


Use Flicker and Truman Show as your models:
  1. Context: Vaping harms mainly the vaper.
  2. Motive: Yet two of the three posters centre a bereaved father and a dead friend.
  3. Framework paragraph: Stylianou's three principles. This is also where you justify why his framework fits the posters.
  4. R1–R3: One reason per kind of harm the posters invoke.
  5. Acknowledgement/response: "Illegal" doesn't fit any of Stylianou's three categories cleanly. Like the Truman essay, treat that gap as evidence, not a problem.

The closest models for your other options:
  • Option 5 (pre- vs post-Aug 2025 posters): Power in Propaganda.
  • Option 8 (earthquake handbooks): Government Involvement. That's also a warning, since the same comparison already exists as a course sample.

Wong Ee Wei, a 29-year-old Singaporean, was sentenced to 25 months' jail and a fine of S$100,000 (US$78,000), while Kenneth Tan Hong Chang, a 31-year-old Singaporean, was given 45 months' jail, a fine of S$36,000 and a driving ban. Tan's Singaporean wife, 30-year-old Tiffany Lim Hui Ping, was sentenced to 18 months' jail and a fine of S$44,000. She was also a member of the syndicate. Wong, who was a leader in the syndicate from mid-2022 to 2024, had earlier pleaded guilty to conspiring to possess vapes for sale and being part of an organised crime group. Tan, who became involved in the syndicate in February 2025, pleaded guilty to similar charges as well as unrelated charges of cheating, misappropriation and traffic-related offences.  His wife pleaded guilty to a charge each for possessing vapes for sale, being part of an organised crime group and allowing a place to be used for crime. THE SYNDICATE From mid-2022 to Oct 16, 2025, the syndicate distributed vapes imported from Malaysia. Comprising syndicate leaders, distributors and area distributors, the syndicate was led by a person believed to be based in Malaysia known as \"Nobody\". # Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order.) When you swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full
gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
2.06:1); on dark, go no darker than **step 600** (`#184f95`, 2.15:1).

## Diverging pair

**blue <-> red** - warm/cool poles that read as opposite. Neutral midpoint is gray
(light `#f0efec`, dark `#383835`). Equal step count per arm. (blue<->aqua was
rejected - both cool, the midpoint doesn't read as "nothing".)

I found 445 headlines in 2025 across the three outlets that mention vapes, Kpods or e-cigarettes: 248 in The Straits Times, 90 on CNA and 107 on Mothership. The chart shows the count for every day, a 7-day average, and monthly totals.
What the data shows
  • January to June were quiet: 55 headlines in six months, about 9 a month.
  • July to September made up two-thirds of the year: 296 headlines, with 75 in July, 128 in August and 93 in September. August alone is about 14 times the earlier monthly rate.
  • The busiest day was 28 August, with 21 headlines. That's when the outlets ran their explainers on the rules starting 1 September, such as "Clampdown on vaping and Kpods: What changes to expect come Sep 1".
  • The build-up starts in mid-July, with headlines like "Singapore working to list etomidate as illegal drug" on 20 July.
  • Coverage falls back after the new rules start: 46 headlines in October, 22 in November and 26 in December. That's still about three times the first-half level, not back to where it was.
  • 98 headlines name Kpods specifically, almost all of them from July onward.

This matches the Google Trends chart you already have, but it measures media coverage rather than public searching.
How I counted
  • Straits Times and CNA: every 2025 result from each site's own search for every term, then kept only results where the term is in the headline itself.
  • Mothership: its own search and API are closed to scripts. I took its 2025 article links from the Internet Archive, kept those with a vape-related term in the link, and fetched each article to read the real headline and date.
  • GDELT, a global news archive I tried first, was rate-limiting this connection, so I didn't use it.

Limitations to mention if you use this in the essay
  • Mothership is probably undercounted. The archive lists about 8,200 of its 2025 articles, which is likely short of the full total, and a headline only gets counted if its link also contains a vape-related term.
  • Headlines that only say "etomidate" aren't counted. For example, "Man charged in first case of driving under the influence of etomidate" is about Kpods but doesn't use the word, so Kpod coverage is understated.
  • CNA's 48 matching videos and audio clips are excluded, to keep all three outlets to written articles. Two Straits Times multimedia pages are excluded for the same reason.
  • Stories about other countries are included. Several are about Malaysia's and Thailand's crackdowns.
  • For your essay: the chart shows that coverage surged around the policy change. It doesn't show that the coverage was coordinated. The instructor has warned against claims of intent that the evidence can't carry, so describe it as a sharp rise in coverage that lined up with the 1 September rules.

Files are in [vape_headlines/](vape_headlines/):
  • [vape_headlines_2025.png](vape_headlines/vape_headlines_2025.png): the chart.
  • [daily_counts_2025.csv](vape_headlines/daily_counts_2025.csv): all 365 days, broken down by outlet.
  • [headlines_2025.csv](vape_headlines/headlines_2025.csv): every counted headline with its date, time and link, plus a Kpod flag.
  • [analyse_plot.py](vape_headlines/analyse_plot.py): re-runs the count and chart if you want to change the search terms.

"""Use Mothership's public Telegram channel (t.me/s/mothershipsg, no login) to find extra 2025 vape-related articles.

1. Binary-search post IDs for the 2025 range, then page through every 2025 post.
2. Keep posts whose text mentions a vape/Kpod/e-cigarette/etomidate term.
3. Follow each post's link to the Mothership article and read the real headline + publish time.
"""
import json, re, time, html, urllib.request, urllib.error, datetime as dt

UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/126 Safari/537.36"
BROAD = re.compile(r"vap(e|es|er|ers|ing)\b|vaporis|k-?pods?\b|e-?cig|etomidate", re.I)


def get(url):
    return urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA}), timeout=60).read().decode("utf-8", "ignore")


def page(before=None):
    """Return [(id, datetime_utc, text, links)] for the 20 posts before `before`."""
    s = get("https://t.me/s/mothershipsg" + (f"?before={before}" if before else ""))
    posts = []

Yes, and you didn't need to log in. Telegram shows public channels at t.me/s/mothershipsg to anyone, and I went through all 4,428 posts the channel made in 2025.
What it changed
  • 65 posts mentioned vapes, Kpods, e-cigarettes or etomidate. I followed each post's link to the Mothership article and read the real headline there.
  • 59 of those 64 articles had already been found through the Internet Archive; one post's link couldn't be followed. So the archive method was catching about 92% of the vape stories Mothership posts to Telegram, which is reassuring.
  • 5 articles were new. Four have a matching headline (in June, August and December). The fifth was a Telegram post that mentioned vapes, but the article itself is about bean sprouts, so it isn't counted.
  • The new total is 449 headlines. Mothership goes from 107 to 111; The Straits Times (248) and CNA (90) are unchanged.
  • The pattern doesn't move. 28 August is still the peak at 21 headlines, and the monthly totals are 75 in July, 129 in August and 93 in September.

What it can't fix
  • It only adds the articles Mothership chose to post. The channel posted 4,428 times in 2025, while the archive lists about 8,200 Mothership articles, so roughly half of Mothership's output never goes on Telegram.
  • Telegram posts aren't headlines. Each post is a rewritten one-line summary, so I only used them to find articles. What's counted is always the headline on the article page.

The chart, [daily_counts_2025.csv](vape_headlines/daily_counts_2025.csv) and [headlines_2025.csv](vape_headlines/headlines_2025.csv) are updated. Each vape-related Telegram post's text and the article it links to are in [tg_vape_posts.json](vape_headlines/tg_vape_posts.json), if you want to quote how Mothership framed these stories on Telegram.

# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -

I've made the chart and saved it as [vape_offences_singapore_2025_2026.png](vape_offences_singapore_2025_2026.png). The script that draws it is [vape_offences_chart.py](vape_offences_chart.py). The official figures cover periods of different lengths (quarters, a 3‑month block, a single month), so I plotted the average number of people caught per month in each period. Each bar is as wide as the period it covers.

Q1 20262,589 (377 etomidate)863
Q2 20262,428 (457 etomidate)809

What it shows:
  • Overall drop: after 1 September 2025 the monthly rate fell by about 30%, from roughly 1,200 to roughly 810–900.
  • Etomidate rising: etomidate (Kpod) offenders went from about 9% of cases in Sep–Nov 2025 to about 19% in Q2 2026. So total offences are falling while the more harmful type is growing.

Limits of the data:
  • HSA only split out etomidate cases from September 2025, so the 2025 bars before that are grey totals.
  • The Q1 and Q2 2025 figures were only published as "more than" 3,100 and 3,700.
  • I worked out the December 2025 figure myself: 3,534 for Sep–Dec minus 2,710 for Sep–Nov.
  • The July–August 2025 bar uses HSA's June–August average because no exact count exists, so it's hatched to show it's approximate.
  • July–September 2026 figures haven't been published yet.

All of this is noted on the chart. If you'd prefer quarterly totals instead of monthly rates, or a simpler version for your essay, I can redraw it.
